Update page titles, H1s, or navigation labels so they match exactly or are clearly consistent variations of the same term. Maintain a navigation-to-page title mapping document and include a title-consistency check in the QA release process.
acceptance_criteria: Every primary navigation item links to a page whose H1 matches or closely mirrors the nav label
Breadcrumb labels match the H1 of the corresponding page
Browser tab title (title tag) is consistent with the page H1
Navigation-to-page-title audit completed for all primary and secondary nav items
Title consistency check included in QA sign-off checklist for all new pages
negative_signals: Navigation label and destination page H1 match or are clearly equivalent
Breadcrumb labels consistent with page H1s
Browser tab title consistent with page H1
issues.context_notes: Click through every primary and secondary navigation item and compare label vs page H1. Do not flag: Minor stylistic variations (e.g., 'Men's Shoes' in nav vs 'Men's Shoes & Trainers' as page H1) that do not create genuine confusion. Industry context: Title mismatches are common after content migrations or CMS restructuring.

issues.issue_title: Inconsistent filter UI patterns across the same site
issues.user_problem: Users must re-learn how to apply filters on different pages because the filter interface uses different patterns (pills, dropdowns, checkboxes) inconsistently
signals_to_detect: One category page uses filter pills while another uses a dropdown panel for equivalent filters
Filter controls use different shapes (rounded vs rectangular) on different pages
Some filter categories show a sidebar panel while others use a top-bar filter approach
Filter interaction behaviour differs across pages (immediate apply vs. apply button required)
issues.recommendation: Standardise all filter interfaces across the site to use a single pattern: define whether filters are presented as a sidebar panel, a top-bar row, or a modal on mobile, and apply this consistently. Standardise the shape, size, and interaction model (immediate apply on selection vs. explicit apply button). Enforce the standard through a shared filter component in the design system rather than page-level implementations.
acceptance_criteria: A single filter pattern used consistently across all PLPs and search results pages
Filter shape (rounded or rectangular), colour, and interaction model identical on all pages
Shared filter component defined in the design system — no page-level custom implementations
Mobile filter pattern consistent across all listing pages (e.g., always a modal, always a drawer)
Filter behaviour (immediate apply vs. apply button) consistent site-wide
negative_signals: Identical filter UI pattern across all PLP and search result pages
Filter shape, size, and interaction model consistent
Filter component sourced from a single design system implementation
issues.context_notes: Compare filter UI across at least 3 different category pages and the search results page. Do not flag: Minor differences in filter content (different attributes per category) — only flag differences in the UI pattern and interaction model. Industry context: Filter inconsistency is particularly confusing for users who switch between product categories.

issues.issue_title: Privacy and data-sharing trust copy missing from sensitive flows
issues.user_problem: Users asked to share personal data (location, contacts, payment details) with third parties have no explanation of how their data will be used or protected
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Third-party sharing flow (social login, location request, payment provider) has no explanation of what data is shared
Location or contact permission request shown without context on why it is needed or how data is used
Checkout step asks for sensitive information with no reassurance copy or privacy link
Gift delivery flow shares recipient details with no statement clarifying data usage
No 'Your data is private' or equivalent reassurance near sensitive input fields
issues.recommendation: Add concise, plain-language privacy reassurance copy at every point where users are asked to share sensitive or personal data. For location sharing: state exactly why the location is needed and confirm it will not be shared with third parties (e.g., 'Your location is only used to calculate delivery — never shared'). For third-party integrations: explain what data will be shared before the user connects. Place this copy immediately adjacent to the relevant field or permission request, not hidden in a privacy policy link.
acceptance_criteria: Every sensitive data input (location, payment, contact details) has adjacent reassurance copy explaining how data is used
Third-party connection flows explain what data is shared before the user authorises
Gift and recipient flows explicitly state that recipient data is not shared with the sender or third parties
Reassurance copy is in plain language — no legalese or policy references as a substitute
Privacy reassurance visible without scrolling at the point of data entry on desktop and mobile
negative_signals: Reassurance copy visible adjacent to all sensitive data entry fields
Third-party integration explains data sharing before user authorises
Recipient/gift flows confirm data confidentiality explicitly
issues.context_notes: Check checkout, account creation, location permission, and any third-party connection flows. Do not flag: Standard footer privacy policy links — these are insufficient substitutes for inline reassurance. Industry context: Trust copy at the point of data entry significantly reduces form abandonment in checkout and registration flows.

issues.issue_title: Hero banner text too small or obscured by overlapping UI elements
issues.user_problem: Users cannot read promotional or informational text on hero banners because it is too small, low contrast, or covered by navigation arrows and overlapping components
signals_to_detect: Banner headline text is smaller than 18px making it difficult to read at normal viewing distance
Carousel navigation arrows positioned over banner text, partially obscuring it
Banner text has insufficient contrast against the background image (fails 4.5:1 ratio)
Promotional text in banner images is not HTML text — embedded in image making it unresizable
Banner content area is too narrow, causing text truncation or wrapping to illegible line lengths
issues.recommendation: Set minimum banner headline font sizes: 28px+ on desktop, 20px+ on mobile. Use HTML text overlaid on CSS background images rather than embedding text inside image files. Apply a semi-transparent dark overlay on busy background images to ensure text contrast meets WCAG 4.5:1. Position carousel navigation arrows in dedicated padding zones outside the content area — never overlapping text. Test banner legibility at arm's length on a mobile device.
acceptance_criteria: Banner headline text minimum 28px on desktop and 20px on mobile
All banner text is HTML/CSS — not embedded in image files
Text on banner background meets WCAG 4.5:1 contrast ratio (use overlay if needed)
Carousel navigation arrows positioned in dedicated zones that do not overlap banner text
Banner text legibility tested on mobile (375px) at arm's length by a team member
negative_signals: Banner headline text clearly readable at normal viewing distance
Navigation arrows in dedicated padding zones not overlapping text
Text contrast passes 4.5:1 against banner background
HTML text used — not embedded in image
issues.context_notes: View homepage and PLP banners on both desktop and mobile. Do not flag: Intentionally minimal hero banners with large, high-contrast text. Industry context: Banner text legibility is directly linked to promotional conversion rates — illegible offers are invisible offers.

issues.issue_title: Carousel end state not communicated to users
issues.user_problem: Users do not know when they have reached the last item in a carousel, causing them to keep clicking the next arrow expecting more content
signals_to_detect: Carousel next arrow remains active and clickable after the last item is reached
No visual end state or stop indicator when the final carousel item is visible
Dot indicators do not highlight the last dot to indicate the final position
Carousel loops silently back to the beginning without indicating the loop
No 'See all' or 'View more' CTA appears when the end of a non-looping carousel is reached
issues.recommendation: Disable and visually grey-out the next arrow when the last carousel item is visible. Highlight the last dot indicator to show final position. For non-looping carousels, show a 'See all [X] items' CTA at the end of the carousel so users have a clear path to view the complete collection. For looping carousels, add a subtle indicator (e.g., 'Back to start') to communicate the loop behaviour.
acceptance_criteria: Next arrow visually disabled (greyed out) when the last carousel item is in view
Dot indicators show the final position clearly when the last slide is active
Non-looping carousels show a 'See all' or 'View more' link at the end
Looping carousels either indicate the loop behaviour or are not looping by default
Keyboard navigation (arrow keys) stops at the last item or clearly wraps with a loop indicator
negative_signals: Next arrow greyed out or hidden when last item is visible
Dot indicators show end position
Non-looping carousels include a 'See all' link at the end
Loop behaviour communicated if carousel wraps
issues.context_notes: Navigate product carousels and content sliders to their last item. Do not flag: Infinite scroll feeds or looping brand carousels where no finite end exists. Industry context: Unclear carousel end states cause users to repeatedly interact with a control that produces no new content, which is frustrating and erodes confidence in the UI.

issues.issue_title: Carousel navigation arrows visible when no overflow exists
issues.user_problem: Users see next/previous arrows on a carousel when all items already fit within the visible area, creating a false affordance that more content exists
signals_to_detect: Carousel shows left/right arrows even when all cards fit within the container without scrolling
Arrow buttons visible and clickable but clicking them produces no movement
3 or fewer items in a carousel designed for 4 columns still shows navigation arrows
Arrows remain visible at viewport sizes where all items are fully visible
issues.recommendation: Conditionally hide carousel navigation arrows when the total number of items does not exceed the number of visible slots. Use JavaScript to compare the scroll width of the carousel track against its container width — if equal or less, hide the arrows. Re-evaluate on window resize using a ResizeObserver. Apply this logic at all responsive breakpoints so arrows don't appear when 4 items are visible on a 4-column desktop layout.
acceptance_criteria: Carousel arrows are hidden when all items fit within the visible container at the current viewport
Arrows appear dynamically when items exceed the visible container width
Arrow visibility re-evaluated on window resize via ResizeObserver
Logic applied at all breakpoints (mobile, tablet, desktop)
No dead-click arrows anywhere on the site — every visible arrow produces a scroll movement
negative_signals: Arrows only visible when carousel content overflows the container
Arrows hidden when all items visible without scrolling
ResizeObserver or equivalent recalculates visibility on resize
issues.context_notes: Test carousels across multiple viewport widths to check arrow visibility vs actual overflow. Do not flag: Deliberately always-visible arrows on large carousels where the exact overflow may vary by 1 item. Industry context: False affordances (arrows that do nothing) undermine interface credibility and are a small but recurring user frustration.

issues.issue_title: Price range filter numbers overlap during interaction
issues.user_problem: When users drag the price range slider handles close together, the minimum and maximum values overlap and become unreadable
signals_to_detect: Min and max price labels overlap when slider handles are dragged close together
Price labels positioned directly above slider handles with no collision detection
Slider value labels flicker or become unreadable when handles are in proximity
No minimum gap enforced between the two slider handles
issues.recommendation: Implement collision detection for price range slider value labels: when the two handles are within a defined pixel distance, merge the labels into a single 'From X to Y' label centred between them, or stack one above the other. Enforce a minimum price gap between handles (e.g., at least the smallest price increment). Alternatively, replace the dual-handle slider with two separate number input fields (min and max) for more precise, collision-free input.
acceptance_criteria: Min and max price labels never visually overlap at any slider position
Collision detection merges or repositions overlapping labels when handles are close
A minimum gap is enforced between the two slider handles
Price values always legible and correctly reflecting the selected range
Alternative number input fields provided as a fallback or replacement for the slider
negative_signals: Price labels never overlap regardless of slider handle position
Collision detection or label merging active
Minimum gap enforced between handles
Values always legible during interaction
issues.context_notes: Test by dragging the min and max price slider handles close together. Do not flag: Price filters implemented as two separate text inputs where overlap is impossible. Industry context: Price range sliders are a frequent ecommerce pattern but the two-handle variant is notoriously prone to UX issues at close range.

issues.issue_title: Excessive brand or logo repetition on the page
issues.user_problem: Repeated display of the same brand logo across multiple sections creates visual noise and cognitive overload, reducing the user's ability to focus on content
signals_to_detect: The same brand logo appears 4 or more times on a single page view
Logo displayed in header, hero banner, mid-page promotional block, and footer simultaneously
Multiple promotional banners on one page each contain the brand logo
Product category pages repeat the brand logo on every product card header
issues.recommendation: Limit brand logo usage to: the site header (primary position), the footer, and one promotional/brand story section if editorially justified. Remove the logo from product cards, mid-page promotional tiles, and any section where its presence adds no informational value — the user is already on the brand's site. Replace logo-heavy promotional blocks with product imagery, offer copy, or social proof content.
acceptance_criteria: Brand logo appears no more than 3 times on any single page (header, footer, one editorial block)
Product cards do not include the brand's own logo
Mid-page promotional tiles use product imagery or offer copy — not a logo repeat
Homepage reviewed and approved with maximum 3 logo placements
Visual hierarchy audit confirms logo repetition does not compete with primary CTAs or content
negative_signals: Logo appears in header, footer, and maximum one editorial block
Product cards free of brand logo repetition
Promotional sections use content — not logo repetition
issues.context_notes: Scroll the full homepage and count logo appearances. Do not flag: Logo appearing in branded product packaging images — this is product content, not UI repetition. Industry context: More common on white-label or franchise sites. Less critical than functional UX issues but contributes to poor visual hierarchy.

issues.issue_title: Images appear stretched or distorted
issues.user_problem: Distorted images make the site look broken and reduce confidence in the product or brand being presented
signals_to_detect: Product or banner images appear visibly stretched or squashed in their containers
Images change aspect ratio when the viewport is resized
object-fit: fill used causing image distortion inside fixed-ratio containers
Images in a grid or carousel have inconsistent aspect ratios causing grid misalignment
Uploaded images of varying native aspect ratios displayed without a consistent crop
issues.recommendation: Apply object-fit: cover to all images displayed within fixed-ratio containers to ensure cropping rather than stretching. Define explicit aspect ratio containers using the padding-top trick or the CSS aspect-ratio property (e.g., aspect-ratio: 4/3) for all image slots. Ensure product image upload guidelines specify a minimum resolution and required aspect ratio so source images are consistent before they reach the front end.
acceptance_criteria: No stretched or distorted images visible on any page at any standard viewport width
object-fit: cover applied to all images in fixed-ratio containers
CSS aspect-ratio or padding-top technique used for all image containers
Product image upload guidelines specify required aspect ratio and minimum resolution
Images tested across viewport widths 320px, 375px, 768px, 1024px, and 1280px — no distortion at any breakpoint
negative_signals: All images maintain correct aspect ratio at all viewports
object-fit: cover confirmed in CSS for image containers
No grid misalignment caused by inconsistent image ratios
issues.context_notes: Resize the browser window across standard breakpoints and look for distorted product, banner, and category images. Do not flag: Intentionally cropped images where only the focal point is shown. Industry context: Stretched images are immediately noticed by users and create a strong impression of low-quality development, particularly on product cards.

issues.issue_title: Brand or product names poorly translated in localised version
issues.user_problem: Localised translations of brand or product names use unfamiliar or incorrect terminology that confuses users and undermines brand trust
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Brand names in navigation or product listings translated into local language using unfamiliar transliterations
Internationally recognised brand names translated when they should remain in their original form
Product category names translated using literal equivalents that do not match local market terminology
Translated brand name differs from how the brand is known and searched for in the local market
issues.recommendation: Review all brand name translations with a native-speaking market specialist. As a default rule: internationally recognised brand names (e.g., Samsung, Nike, Apple) should remain untranslated in their original form. Only translate brand names when the brand has an officially localised name in the target market. For product category names, validate translations with native users via a card sort or preference test to confirm the chosen terminology matches local search behaviour.
acceptance_criteria: All internationally recognised brand names kept in original form — not translated
Product category name translations validated by a native market specialist
Translated terminology matches terms used in local market search behaviour (verified via search volume data)
Translation review process includes a native speaker sign-off before publishing
Users in the target market can identify all brand and category names without confusion (tested with 5 native users)
negative_signals: International brand names kept in original form throughout
Category name translations validated by native speakers
Translated terminology matches local search and market language
issues.context_notes: Requires native language review — flag for specialist validation rather than making translation judgements without local market knowledge. Do not flag: Brands that have an official localised name in the target market (e.g., some brands have officially registered Arabic names). Industry context: Particularly important for Arabic, Chinese, and RTL market localisation.

issues.issue_title: Inconsistent filter shape language on the same page
issues.user_problem: Filters using both rounded pill shapes and rectangular shapes on the same page create a visual inconsistency that implies different behaviours or categories of filter
signals_to_detect: Filter tags or chips use rounded/pill style in one section and rectangular style in another on the same page
Active filter chips use a different shape from inactive filter options
Quick filter bar at top uses pill style while the filter panel sidebar uses rectangular checkboxes with different border-radius
Filter shape inconsistency present across different category pages on the same site
issues.recommendation: Standardise filter shape language across the entire site: choose either rounded pills or rectangular chips and apply consistently to all filter elements — quick filters, filter panels, active filter chips, and mobile filter drawers. Document the chosen filter shape in the design system. Ensure active and inactive states use the same shape and differ only in fill colour, border, and label weight.
acceptance_criteria: All filter elements (quick filters, panel options, active chips) use the same border-radius value
Filter shape consistent across all PLPs, search results, and mobile filter views
Active and inactive filter states differ only in fill/border colour — same shape
Filter shape documented in design system with specific border-radius token
No mix of rounded pills and rectangular chips on any single page
negative_signals: All filter elements use the same border-radius across the page
Shape consistent between quick filter bar and filter panel
Active and inactive filter chips use identical shape
issues.context_notes: Compare quick filter bar, filter panel, and active filter chips on the same page. Do not flag: Intentional shape differentiation where rounded = multi-select and rectangular = single-select, if this convention is applied consistently. Industry context: Filter shape inconsistency is a visual polish issue — lower priority than functional filter problems but contributes to perceived quality.

issues.issue_title: Floating button label or text obscured by overlapping element
issues.user_problem: Text or labels on floating action buttons (WhatsApp, live chat, back to top) are covered by other page elements, making them unreadable or the button purpose unclear
signals_to_detect: WhatsApp, chat, or other floating button label text is cut off or hidden behind another element
Floating button tooltip or label covered by sticky header, footer bar, or another fixed element
Floating button z-index lower than overlapping page elements
On mobile, floating button hidden behind the browser's bottom navigation bar or iOS safe area
issues.recommendation: Ensure all floating action buttons have a z-index higher than all other fixed or sticky elements on the page. Add bottom padding or safe-area-inset-bottom CSS variable to account for iOS and Android browser chrome. Test floating button visibility at all standard viewport sizes and on real mobile devices. If a floating button label is frequently obscured, convert the label to a tooltip that appears on hover/tap rather than always-on text.
acceptance_criteria: Floating button fully visible and label legible at all standard viewport sizes
Floating button z-index higher than all sticky headers, banners, and footer bars
Bottom floating buttons respect iOS safe area (env(safe-area-inset-bottom))
Floating button tested on iOS Safari and Android Chrome — no occlusion
Button label or tooltip readable without any element overlapping it
negative_signals: Floating button fully visible and unobscured on all tested viewports
z-index higher than all other fixed elements confirmed in CSS
iOS safe area inset applied to bottom-positioned buttons
issues.context_notes: Check bottom-fixed floating buttons on mobile viewport (375px) and on a real iOS device. Do not flag: Floating buttons that are intentionally hidden on scroll (scroll-away behaviour). Industry context: WhatsApp and live chat floating buttons are extremely common in Middle East ecommerce; occlusion is a frequent implementation bug.

issues.issue_title: Step indicator uses colour incorrectly — pending and complete states indistinguishable
issues.user_problem: Users misread their progress in a multi-step flow because the colour used for pending steps (not yet reached) is the same as or similar to the colour used for completed steps
signals_to_detect: Green colour used for both completed steps and upcoming/pending steps in a progress indicator
Active (current) step visually indistinguishable from completed steps
Pending steps appear highlighted or coloured in a way that implies they are already done
No clear visual differentiation between completed, current, and upcoming step states
issues.recommendation: Define three visually distinct states for step indicators: (1) Completed — green fill with a checkmark icon; (2) Current/Active — brand primary colour fill or bold outline with the step number; (3) Pending/Upcoming — grey or muted outline with the step number. Never use green for pending steps. Apply the same three-state system consistently to checkout, onboarding, and all multi-step form flows.
acceptance_criteria: Completed steps use green fill with a visible checkmark icon
Current step uses a visually distinct active colour (brand primary or bold outline)
Pending/upcoming steps use grey or muted outline — never green or a colour implying completion
Three states are visually distinguishable in greyscale as well as colour (not colour-only differentiation)
Step indicator states consistent across all multi-step flows (checkout, registration, onboarding)
negative_signals: Completed, current, and pending steps each use visually distinct styling
Green reserved for completed steps only
States distinguishable in greyscale
issues.context_notes: Check checkout progress indicator and any onboarding or registration step flows. Do not flag: Step indicators that use numbered circles with clear label states even if colour alone is ambiguous — flag only when all three states are genuinely confusable. Industry context: Step colour confusion is particularly common in government and banking digital services.

issues.issue_title: Time or unit label mismatch in content or UI
issues.user_problem: Users are shown a label (e.g., 'hours') that does not match the actual value or unit used (e.g., the value is in days), creating confusion about timelines, delivery windows, or service parameters
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Field or label says 'hours' but value displayed is expressed in days
Delivery or processing time displayed in the wrong unit relative to its label
Form field label says 'minutes' but accepted input is in seconds
Service duration or SLA stated in a unit inconsistent with user expectation or actual value
ETA or countdown uses a unit mismatch that makes the time unclear
issues.recommendation: Audit all time, duration, and unit-based labels across the interface against the actual values they represent. Update labels to accurately reflect the unit of the value displayed (e.g., change 'Service Request Hours' to 'Processing Time' or 'Business Days'). Use flexible, future-proof labels where values may vary (e.g., 'Estimated time' rather than 'Hours') to prevent recurring mismatches as content is updated.
acceptance_criteria: All time and duration labels accurately describe the unit of the adjacent value
No instance of 'hours' label used when value is in days (or vice versa)
Labels reviewed and corrected across all service description, checkout, and account pages
Flexible label conventions used (e.g., 'Processing time') where unit may vary
Content review process includes a unit-consistency check for all time-related copy
negative_signals: All labels accurately reflect the unit of the displayed value
No hours/days or minutes/seconds mismatches present
Time labels reviewed and approved as part of content QA
issues.context_notes: Check service pages, delivery information, form field labels, and any SLA or processing time content. Do not flag: Approximate labels ('a few hours', 'same day') where precision is intentionally avoided. Industry context: Unit mismatches are common in government, banking, and logistics-heavy ecommerce where service timelines are managed separately from UI copy.

issues.issue_title: First-person language used in instructional or step-based copy
issues.user_problem: Instructions written in first person ('I would like to…') confuse users about whether they are reading a prompt to complete or a statement the system is making on their behalf
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Step descriptions use 'I would like to…' or 'I want to…' instead of instructional language
Process steps written in first person as if the system is expressing the user's intent
Instructional copy and user-voice copy mixed on the same page without clear differentiation
Onboarding or service request steps read as user statements rather than system instructions
issues.recommendation: Rewrite all instructional and step-based copy in second person ('You will need to…') or imperative form ('Enter your details', 'Select a delivery date'). Reserve first-person language exclusively for contexts where the user is explicitly composing a message or making a choice that will be attributed to them (e.g., a confirmation checkbox: 'I agree to the terms'). Establish this as a content style rule in the writing guide.
acceptance_criteria: All instructional and step-based copy uses second person or imperative voice — not first person
No step label or instruction begins with 'I would like to', 'I want to', or 'I need to'
First-person language reserved only for explicit user-authored content (checkboxes, written reviews)
Content style guide updated to include the first-person/imperative distinction rule
All existing step-based content reviewed and corrected across service flows and onboarding
negative_signals: All instructional copy uses second person or imperative form
No first-person step descriptions present
Content style guide defines voice rules for instructional copy
issues.context_notes: Check service request flows, onboarding steps, and checkout instructions. Do not flag: Confirmation copy where first person is appropriate ('I confirm I am over 18', 'I agree to the terms'). Industry context: First-person instructional copy is a common error in multilingual sites where direct translations from Arabic or other languages introduce first-person constructs that work in the source language but read oddly in English.

issues.issue_title: Chatbot or automated support creates circular navigation without resolution
issues.user_problem: Users contacting support via chatbot or automated phone system are routed in loops and cannot reach a human or resolve their issue, causing abandonment and frustration
nielsen_heuristic: Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors
signals_to_detect: Chatbot responds to unrecognised queries with a generic fallback and restarts the same menu loop
No clear path to a human agent from within the chatbot flow
Chatbot offers only pre-defined topic options that do not match the user's actual issue
Support phone IVR routes users back to the main menu after each option without resolving the issue
Time to reach a human agent exceeds 5 minutes from first contact attempt
issues.recommendation: Redesign the chatbot and IVR flow to include an explicit 'Speak to a human' or 'None of these' escape route at every decision point — never more than 2 steps from a live agent or a ticket submission. Implement intent recognition (NLP) so the bot can handle unscripted queries rather than only pre-defined topics. Set a fallback rule: if the same user has cycled through 2 or more bot loops without resolution, automatically escalate to a human handoff or offer a callback. Measure containment rate and escalation rate monthly.
acceptance_criteria: A 'Talk to a human' or 'Contact us directly' option visible at every chatbot menu level
Users can reach a live agent or submit a support ticket within 2 interactions from any point in the chat
Chatbot handles free-text input with intent recognition — not only scripted button flows
If a user loops through 2+ bot flows without resolution, escalation to human is automatically offered
Average time to human handoff under 3 minutes measured over 30-day sample
negative_signals: Clear 'Talk to a human' option visible at all chatbot menu levels
Free-text chatbot input handled meaningfully rather than defaulting to menu restart
Escalation to human offered after 2 failed resolution attempts
Time to human contact under 3 minutes
issues.context_notes: Test by contacting support with an unusual or complex query not covered by the standard menu options. Do not flag: Simple FAQ chatbots on low-complexity sites where most queries are genuinely self-service. Industry context: Circular chatbot navigation is a top-3 customer service complaint across ecommerce, banking, and telecoms. The frustration amplifies post-purchase when users have urgent order or delivery issues.

issues.issue_title: Cross-channel inconsistency — different answers from different support touchpoints
issues.user_problem: Users receive conflicting information depending on whether they contact support via chat, email, or phone, destroying trust and forcing repeat contacts
signals_to_detect: Customer receives a different answer about a policy, order status, or offer from chat vs email vs phone
Agent in one channel is unaware of a commitment made by an agent in another channel
Support team has no access to previous interaction history when a customer contacts them
Promotions or offers communicated verbally but not confirmed in writing via email or in-account
Order or account status shown differently in the app vs what a phone agent states
issues.recommendation: Implement a unified CRM so every customer-facing channel (chat, email, phone, in-app) shares a single view of customer history, commitments, and status. Ensure all promotions, offers, and commitments made verbally or in chat are automatically followed up with a written confirmation (email or in-app notification). Train all support agents on the same knowledge base and policy documents. Define a single source of truth for order and account status that all channels read from.
acceptance_criteria: All support channels have access to the same customer interaction history via a unified CRM
Any offer or commitment made in a support interaction triggers an automatic written confirmation to the customer
Order and account status is identical across app, website, and agent view at the same point in time
Support agents can see previous interactions across all channels before responding
Cross-channel consistency tested monthly by submitting the same query via 3 channels and comparing responses
negative_signals: All channels access the same customer history and status data
Commitments followed up with written confirmation automatically
Order/account status consistent between app and agent system
No reported cases of conflicting channel responses
issues.context_notes: Test by submitting the same order or policy query via chat, then phone, and comparing responses. Do not flag: Minor tone or wording differences between channels that convey the same information. Industry context: Cross-channel inconsistency is cited as the #1 trust-destroying experience in banking and high-AOV ecommerce. Particularly damaging when it involves refunds, promotions, or delivery commitments.

issues.issue_title: Verbal or in-chat commitments not confirmed in writing
issues.user_problem: Users who receive a promise (discount, upgrade, delivery guarantee) from a support agent have no written record, leaving them unable to claim or reference it later
signals_to_detect: Support agent makes a commitment (e.g., 'I'll apply a discount to your next order') but no email or in-account record is created
Promotional offers communicated via phone with no confirmation email sent automatically
Users told to 'register for the offer' separately after it was verbally agreed
Chat transcripts not emailed to the customer after a support session ends
Order changes agreed in support interaction not visible in the customer's order history
issues.recommendation: Automate the generation of a written confirmation for any commitment made during a support interaction: offer discounts applied to account immediately and confirmed via email, chat transcripts emailed to the customer at session end, and any agreed service changes reflected in the customer's account within 15 minutes. Build confirmation workflows into the CRM so agents cannot close a ticket without triggering the relevant confirmation communication.
acceptance_criteria: Chat transcript automatically emailed to the customer within 5 minutes of session end
Any discount, credit, or offer applied by an agent is immediately reflected in the customer's account and confirmed via email
Support ticket closure triggers an email summary of the resolution and any commitments made
Agents cannot mark a commitment as given without triggering the automated confirmation workflow
Customer can view support interaction history and outcomes in their account dashboard
negative_signals: Chat transcripts sent to customer email automatically at session end
Discounts and commitments reflected in account within 15 minutes
Support interaction history visible in customer account
Confirmation email sent for any agent-applied offer or change
issues.context_notes: Test by requesting a discount or policy exception from a support agent and checking whether a written confirmation is automatically issued. Do not flag: Brief informational queries where no commitment is made. Industry context: Commitment-without-confirmation is a regulatory risk in banking and a significant trust issue in ecommerce. It disproportionately affects high-value customers making complex purchases.

issues.issue_title: Digital onboarding steps unclear — requirements not communicated upfront
issues.user_problem: Users begin an account creation or registration process without knowing what documents, information, or verification steps are required, causing drop-off mid-flow
signals_to_detect: Account creation or registration flow begins without a summary of required information (documents, verification, eligibility)
Users encounter a step requiring ID verification, phone number, or document upload without prior warning
No estimated completion time or step count shown before the user begins the registration flow
Required fields or documents only revealed mid-flow or after the user has invested significant time
Eligibility requirements (age, country, account type) not stated before the form begins
issues.recommendation: Add a pre-onboarding summary screen before the registration flow begins, listing: all required information and documents, estimated time to complete, eligibility requirements, and what happens after completion. Use a 'What you'll need' checklist pattern so users can prepare before starting. Ensure no new requirement is introduced mid-flow that wasn't in the upfront summary.
acceptance_criteria: A 'What you'll need' summary screen or checklist shown before registration begins
All required documents, fields, and verification steps listed upfront
Estimated completion time stated before the flow begins
Eligibility requirements stated before the first form step
No new requirement introduced in the middle of the flow that was not in the upfront summary
negative_signals: Pre-flow summary lists all required documents and steps
Estimated completion time shown before registration begins
Eligibility requirements stated upfront
No mid-flow surprises — all requirements known in advance
issues.context_notes: Test by beginning the account creation or KYC flow and noting any requirements revealed mid-flow that were not in an upfront summary. Do not flag: Simple email/password registration with no ID or document requirements. Industry context: Applies strongly to fintech, banking, and regulated ecommerce. Also relevant for B2B account creation, seller onboarding, and any flow requiring document upload.

issues.issue_title: Active order or session status not visible — users cannot self-serve status checks
issues.user_problem: Users with active orders, subscriptions, or service sessions cannot see their current status from the app or account area and must contact support to find out
signals_to_detect: Active order status (processing, shipped, out for delivery) not visible in account without navigating multiple levels
No live tracking or progress indicator for ongoing orders or service sessions
Users must call or contact support to find out the current status of an active order or booking
Account dashboard does not surface active sessions, upcoming renewals, or pending actions
Status updates require a page refresh rather than updating in real time or near-real time
issues.recommendation: Surface active order and session status on the account dashboard homepage as the primary widget — showing order number, current status, estimated resolution/delivery, and a tracking link. For time-sensitive statuses (out for delivery, booking confirmed), trigger a push notification or email at each status change. Ensure the status shown in-app matches the status visible to support agents in real time.
acceptance_criteria: Active order or service status visible on the account dashboard without navigating to a sub-page
Status shows current stage, estimated delivery/completion, and a tracking link where applicable
Push notification or email sent at each major status change (e.g., dispatched, out for delivery, delivered)
Status in-app matches what support agents can see in their system at the same moment
Users can self-serve status checks without contacting support for standard order or service queries
negative_signals: Active order status visible on account dashboard homepage
Real-time or near-real time status updates shown
Push or email notifications sent at each status change
Status consistent between customer-facing app and support agent view
issues.context_notes: Test by placing an order and checking whether its status is prominently visible on the account dashboard without drilling into menus. Do not flag: Sites where the only orders are digital/instant and real-time status is irrelevant. Industry context: 'Where is my order?' is the single highest-volume support contact reason across ecommerce — visible status tracking directly reduces support cost.

issues.issue_title: No proactive notifications for upcoming renewals, reminders, or required actions
issues.user_problem: Users miss subscription renewals, payment deadlines, or required actions because the platform only shows this information passively in the account area rather than proactively notifying them
signals_to_detect: Subscription renewal date not surfaced in the account dashboard or via notification
No email or push notification sent before a recurring payment is charged
Required account actions (e.g., document expiry, verification renewal) only visible when user logs in and navigates to the relevant section
No reminders sent for items left in cart, wishlist, or saved for later
Upcoming delivery date not communicated proactively — user must check the order page manually
issues.recommendation: Implement a notification system with opt-in email and push notifications for: subscription renewals (7 days and 1 day before), upcoming deliveries (24 hours before estimated arrival), cart abandonment (1 hour and 24 hours after), wishlist price drops, required account actions (30 days before expiry), and payment reminders (3 days before due). Show a notification bell icon in the account header that surfaces unread notifications.
acceptance_criteria: Subscription renewal notification sent via email at least 7 days before the charge date
Delivery notification sent at dispatch and 24 hours before estimated arrival
Cart abandonment notification sent 1 hour and 24 hours after items are left in cart (for opted-in users)
Required account actions (document expiry, verification) surfaced via notification 30+ days before the deadline
Notification centre or bell icon in account header showing unread notifications
negative_signals: Renewal reminders sent proactively via email before charge date
Delivery notifications sent at key milestones
Account actions surfaced via notification before deadlines
Notification centre visible in account header
issues.context_notes: Check account area for notification preferences and test by setting up a subscription or future delivery and observing whether proactive notifications are sent. Do not flag: One-time purchase sites with no subscriptions or renewals. Industry context: Proactive renewal notifications are both a user experience requirement and a regulatory expectation in many subscription and financial contexts.

issues.issue_title: Dispute or complaint resolution unavailable through digital self-service
issues.user_problem: Users who need to raise a complaint, dispute a charge, or escalate an issue cannot do so through the app or website and are forced to call or visit in person
signals_to_detect: No 'Dispute', 'Report a problem', or 'Raise a complaint' option visible in the account or order management area
Refund or dispute requests only possible by calling or emailing — not through the digital channel
Order issue reporting form absent or leads only to a generic contact form with no case tracking
Users who submit a complaint receive no case reference number or status tracking
No self-service route to escalate an unresolved issue to a senior or specialist team
issues.recommendation: Add a 'Report a problem' or 'Raise a dispute' action to all order and transaction pages in the account. The flow should: capture the issue type, allow photo/file attachment, generate a case reference number, provide an estimated response time, and allow the user to track case status in their account. Send a confirmation email with the case reference immediately on submission.
acceptance_criteria: 'Report a problem' or 'Raise a dispute' action available on every order or transaction in the account
Dispute submission generates a unique case reference number shown on screen and emailed to the user
Estimated response time communicated at time of submission
Case status trackable from the account without contacting support
Photo and file attachment supported in the dispute form for evidence submission
negative_signals: 'Report a problem' option visible on order and transaction pages
Case reference number generated and emailed on submission
Case status trackable in account without contacting support
Estimated response time communicated upfront
issues.context_notes: Check the order detail page and account settings for any dispute or complaint option. Do not flag: Sites where the 'Report a problem' button exists but links to a contact form — note as partial implementation. Industry context: Digital dispute resolution is a consumer protection requirement in many jurisdictions and a key driver of NPS in ecommerce, banking, and services.

issues.issue_title: Search field has unclear clear/delete icon and competing search CTAs
issues.user_problem: Users who make a typing mistake in the search field struggle to find and tap the delete/clear icon, and multiple competing icons or buttons create cognitive load when all they want to do is search
signals_to_detect: Search field has no visible X or clear icon to delete entered text
Clear icon present but too small (under 20px) or low contrast, making it hard to spot
Multiple icon buttons adjacent to the search input (voice, camera, filter, clear) with no clear hierarchy
More than one button appears to initiate search, creating ambiguity about which to tap
Tapping the clear icon does not immediately remove all entered text
issues.recommendation: Show a single prominent clear/X icon inside the search input field on the right side, appearing as soon as the user types any character. Ensure the icon is at least 24px with sufficient contrast. Audit the search bar for any competing icons — retain only those serving distinct, essential purposes and remove or move any that could be confused with the search submit action. The submit/search action should be a single unambiguous trigger (enter key or magnifier icon).
acceptance_criteria: A clear/X icon appears inside the search field as soon as the user types at least one character
Clear icon minimum 24px with 3:1 contrast ratio against the input field background
Tapping the clear icon removes all text and returns focus to the input field immediately
No more than one submit trigger (enter key or magnifier) — no competing search initiation buttons
Search icon row audited — all visible icons serve distinct, labelled purposes with no ambiguity about which initiates search
negative_signals: Visible, well-sized X icon appears when search field contains text
Single unambiguous search submit trigger present
No competing icons of equal visual weight adjacent to search input
Clear icon removes all text on first tap
issues.context_notes: Test by typing into the search field and attempting to clear it. Do not flag: Search fields where the clear icon appears on hover only on desktop — this is acceptable if touch/mobile shows it always-on. Industry context: Particularly frustrating on mobile where correcting a mis-typed search requires precise tapping of a tiny target.

issues.issue_title: Background feature state not confirmed to user — setting active but silent
issues.user_problem: Users enable a background feature (notifications, location, auto-save, voice) but receive no confirmation that it is active, leaving them uncertain whether the setting took effect
signals_to_detect: Toggling a notification, location, or auto-save setting shows no confirmation that the change was applied
Feature is enabled in settings but gives no indication it is active when the user is using it
Users turn a feature on, navigate away, return, and cannot tell if it is still active
Toggle switches change visually but no success message, toast, or status indicator confirms the save
Feature dependent on a background permission (location, push) activates silently with no onboarding prompt explaining it is now running
issues.recommendation: For every toggle or setting that activates a background feature: (1) show an immediate inline confirmation (toast or status badge) confirming the change was saved; (2) display a persistent visible status indicator in the relevant UI area showing the feature is active (e.g., a location pin filled vs outlined, a bell icon with a dot); (3) on first activation, show a brief onboarding prompt explaining what the feature does and how to turn it off.
acceptance_criteria: Toggling any setting shows a toast or inline confirmation within 500ms confirming the change
Features active in the background display a visible persistent status indicator in the relevant UI
First-time activation of a background feature triggers a brief explanation of what it does
Returning to a page with an active background feature shows its status without requiring the user to open settings
Settings that fail to save (e.g., due to network error) show an error state — not silent failure
negative_signals: Setting change confirmed with toast or inline message immediately
Active background features show a persistent status indicator
First activation includes a brief contextual explanation
Failed saves show an error — no silent failures
issues.context_notes: Test by toggling notification preferences, location sharing, or auto-save and checking whether any confirmation is shown. Do not flag: Simple on/off toggles where the visual toggle state alone is sufficient feedback (e.g., dark mode). Flag specifically when the feature has delayed or invisible effects that the toggle state alone cannot communicate.

issues.issue_title: Inconsistent or unreliable feature behaviour erodes user trust
issues.user_problem: A feature that works correctly some of the time but fails unpredictably causes users to stop trusting and using it, even when it is working
signals_to_detect: A feature produces correct output on some interactions and incorrect or no output on others with no change in user input
Users report or testing reveals the same action producing different results on repeated attempts
Feature shows degraded behaviour under normal conditions (average network, standard device) — not only edge cases
Error states for the feature are silent — failure produces no feedback, making the issue invisible
Users have developed workarounds for a feature that should work reliably (e.g., refreshing to trigger a function)
issues.recommendation: Instrument the feature with error monitoring (e.g., Sentry) and logging to capture failure rate, failure conditions, and affected devices/browsers. Set a reliability SLA (e.g., 99% success rate under standard conditions) and treat failures below this as P1 bugs. Add explicit error states with recovery actions so failures are visible rather than silent. Run regression tests covering the feature under varied network conditions (3G, throttled, offline) before each release.
acceptance_criteria: Feature produces consistent output on 99%+ of interactions under standard conditions
All feature failures produce a visible error state with a recovery action — no silent failures
Error monitoring in place tracking feature-specific failure rate and conditions
Regression test suite covers the feature under varied network and device conditions
Feature reliability measured and reported in the QA dashboard before each release
negative_signals: Feature produces correct output consistently across repeated interactions
Failures produce visible error states with recovery options
Error monitoring active and tracking failure rate
Regression tests confirm reliability before release
issues.context_notes: Test by repeating the same action 5–10 times and observing consistency of output. Do not flag: Features that degrade only under extreme conditions (no connectivity, very old devices) — flag only inconsistency under normal, expected conditions. Industry context: Intermittent failures are more damaging to trust than consistent failures because users cannot predict or plan around them.

issues.issue_title: Redundant UI duplication — same information shown twice with no differentiation
issues.user_problem: The same piece of information or UI element appears twice in the same view without any difference in meaning or purpose, creating confusion about whether the two instances mean something different
signals_to_detect: The same label, icon, or data value appears twice on the same screen with identical content
Two badge, tag, or chip elements on a product card show the same category or attribute
A section heading and a nearby label both display the same text without meaningful distinction
Two CTAs of identical label placed close together on the same screen
The same status indicator shown in two locations simultaneously (e.g., in the header and inline) with no contextual difference
issues.recommendation: Audit all key page templates for duplicate information or UI elements. For each duplicate, determine the intended purpose — if both instances serve the same purpose, remove one. If they serve different purposes, differentiate them visually and semantically (different label, different visual weight, different position in the hierarchy) so users understand why both exist. Apply the rule: every piece of information should appear exactly once in a given context unless repetition serves a specific, justified purpose (e.g., a CTA repeated at top and bottom of a long page).
acceptance_criteria: No page template shows the same label, icon, or value twice in the same view without differentiation
Duplicated CTAs reviewed — identical-label CTAs in close proximity removed or differentiated
Product cards and listing items audited for duplicate badge or tag content
Any justified repetitions (e.g., CTA at top and bottom of long page) documented with rationale
Page audit conducted across homepage, PLP, PDP, cart, and account — zero unintentional duplicates
negative_signals: No identical labels or values duplicated in the same view
CTAs with identical labels not placed in close proximity without differentiation
Product card attributes show each piece of information once only
issues.context_notes: Scan each page by looking for repeated text, icons, or values in the same viewport. Do not flag: Justified repetition with a clear purpose (e.g., order total shown in both the summary and the payment form). Industry context: Redundant UI often originates from multiple teams contributing to the same component or from iterative feature additions without a holistic page review.

issues.issue_title: Colour coding system does not match user mental model
issues.user_problem: The colour used to represent a status or category contradicts users' existing expectations (e.g., yellow meaning 'caution' used for a positive state), causing misinterpretation and decision errors
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Green used for a negative or warning state; red used for a positive state
Yellow or amber used for a high-severity status where users expect red
Status colours inconsistent across the same site (green means 'active' on one page, 'pending' on another)
Colour coding for stock levels, order status, or payment states contradicts standard traffic-light conventions (red=stop/danger, green=go/safe, amber=caution)
Custom colour system used without a legend or key, forcing users to guess meanings
issues.recommendation: Align status colour coding with universally understood conventions: red for errors, danger, or unavailability; green for success, active, or available; amber/yellow for warnings, pending, or low-stock caution states. Audit all status indicators, badges, tags, and progress elements across the site and standardise them to this system. Where a custom colour must be used, add a text label so the meaning is never colour-dependent alone (supporting colour-blind users).
acceptance_criteria: Red used exclusively for errors, danger, out-of-stock, or negative states
Green used exclusively for success, active, available, or positive states
Amber/yellow used exclusively for warnings, pending, or caution states
Colour coding consistent for the same status type across all page templates
All status colours supplemented with a text label — meaning never conveyed by colour alone
negative_signals: Red, green, and amber used consistently with standard conventions
Same status type uses the same colour across all pages
All colour-coded statuses include a text label
No colour used for a state that contradicts user expectations
issues.context_notes: Review stock level badges, order status indicators, form validation states, and promotional tags. Do not flag: Brand colour use in non-status contexts (e.g., a red brand CTA button does not imply danger). Industry context: Colour semantic mismatches are particularly damaging in checkout and order management where users make financial decisions based on status colours.

issues.issue_title: Same colour used for two different system states causing ambiguity
issues.user_problem: Users cannot distinguish between two different states (e.g., 'closed' and 'offline') because they are represented by the same colour, forcing them to read labels or context to determine meaning
signals_to_detect: Grey used for both 'disabled/inactive' and 'unavailable/closed' states with no visual differentiation
The same colour applied to 'sold out', 'coming soon', and 'discontinued' product states on the same page
Active and visited link states share the same colour
Two distinct filter states (applied vs available) use the same hue with only a minor shade difference that is not perceptible to all users
Pending and completed states use the same colour in a progress or order flow
issues.recommendation: Conduct a colour-state audit across all interactive and status elements. For any colour used for more than one semantically distinct state, assign a unique visual treatment to each: differentiate by hue, saturation, pattern, icon, or text label. Use a state-to-colour mapping document in the design system to enforce uniqueness. As a rule: no two different states should be visually indistinguishable when a text label is not present.
acceptance_criteria: Each distinct system state uses a unique visual treatment (colour, icon, pattern, or combination)
No two semantically different states are represented by the same colour without an additional differentiator
State-to-colour mapping documented in the design system
All states distinguishable in greyscale as well as colour (pattern or icon as backup differentiator)
Colour-state audit completed across product availability, order status, and filter states
negative_signals: Each distinct state uses a unique and identifiable visual treatment
State-to-colour mapping documented in design system
States distinguishable in greyscale
No colour ambiguity between distinct states on any page
issues.context_notes: Look at product availability states (in stock, low stock, out of stock, discontinued) and order/filter states on the same page. Do not flag: Minor shade differences that are intentional and clearly distinguishable (e.g., lighter and darker green for two positive states). Industry context: Colour ambiguity compounds for users with colour vision deficiency — affects ~8% of male users globally.

issues.issue_title: In-page advertisements disruptive and navigate users away from their task
issues.user_problem: Advertisements displayed within product or content pages interrupt the user's primary task, and tapping them accidentally navigates users out of the app or page, causing frustration and loss of context
signals_to_detect: Advertisements injected within product listings or content pages interrupt the browsing flow
Tapping an ad navigates the user out of the current app or page to an external destination without warning
Ads placed adjacent to primary CTAs (Add to Cart, Next, Submit) causing accidental taps
No 'Ad' or 'Sponsored' label distinguishing ads from organic product content
Ads auto-expanding or overlaying content, requiring user action to dismiss before continuing
issues.recommendation: Position all advertisements in clearly demarcated zones that do not interrupt the primary task flow — never between product cards in a grid, adjacent to purchase CTAs, or overlaying content. Label all ads clearly with 'Ad' or 'Sponsored'. Ensure ad taps open content in-app or in a new tab — never navigating away from the current page without a back route. Consider removing ads from high-intent pages (cart, checkout, PDP) entirely, as ad revenue is outweighed by conversion loss.
acceptance_criteria: All ads clearly labelled with 'Ad' or 'Sponsored' badge
Ads positioned in dedicated zones — not between product listings or adjacent to purchase CTAs
Ad taps open destination in a new tab or in-app browser — not replacing the current page
No ads on cart, checkout, or payment pages
Ad placements audited to ensure no accidental tap risk adjacent to primary interactive elements
negative_signals: All ads clearly labelled and in dedicated zones
Ad taps open in new tab — not replacing current page
No ads on cart or checkout pages
No accidental tap risk from ad placement near CTAs
issues.context_notes: Check ad placements on PLP, PDP, and homepage. Do not flag: Clearly labelled sponsored product listings within a search results grid where the format is consistent with organic results. Industry context: Ad-click-navigating-away is particularly severe on mobile where misplaced ads near scroll areas and CTAs cause frequent accidental interactions.

issues.issue_title: Icon interaction produces no visible change — user unsure if action registered
issues.user_problem: Users tap or click an icon expecting a visible response, but the interface produces no perceptible feedback, leaving them uncertain whether their action was registered
signals_to_detect: Tapping an icon (filter, sort, share, wishlist, toggle) produces no visible change in the icon or surrounding UI
Icon changes colour subtly on tap but the change is too small to perceive at a glance
Toggle icons have no visual active/inactive state distinction
Interactive icon lacks a ripple, colour change, or state animation on tap/click
Users repeat-tap an icon because they cannot tell if the first tap was registered
issues.recommendation: Ensure every interactive icon has a distinct, immediately perceptible active state that differs clearly from its default state — use a combination of fill vs outline, colour change, background highlight, or a brief animation (scale or ripple). The state change should be perceivable within 100ms of the interaction. For toggle icons, the active state should be clearly different in both colour and form (not just a hue shift).
acceptance_criteria: Every interactive icon has a visually distinct active/pressed state that differs from its default
Active state change perceivable within 100ms of tap or click
Toggle icons differ in both colour and form (e.g., filled vs outline heart for wishlist)
Icons with a loading state (e.g., adding to cart) show a brief spinner or progress indicator
Active icon states pass 3:1 contrast ratio between active and inactive visual treatments
negative_signals: All interactive icons have a clearly perceptible active state
State change visible within 100ms of interaction
Toggle icons distinguish active/inactive by both colour and form
No icon interaction produces a silent, imperceptible response
issues.context_notes: Test by tapping all icon-only interactive elements (wishlist, filter, sort, share, toggle) and observing the visual response. Do not flag: Icons with hover states only on desktop where tap response is provided by native mobile press feedback. Industry context: Invisible icon feedback is a frequent cause of repeat-tapping and accidental duplicate actions (e.g., adding an item to cart twice).

issues.issue_title: Missing POI or destination data in platform database
issues.user_problem: Users cannot find a known destination, venue, or product because it is missing from the platform's database, forcing them to use workarounds or switch to a competitor
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Searching for a known, real destination or item returns zero results or a 'not found' state
Users resort to entering a nearby address or landmark as a workaround for a missing primary destination
Competitor platforms (Google Maps, Amazon, etc.) successfully return the same search with correct results
Users report switching to a competitor specifically because the platform couldn't find what they were looking for
No 'Report a missing place' or 'Suggest a listing' option available to users who encounter the gap
issues.recommendation: Conduct a systematic data completeness audit comparing the platform's database against a competitor or authoritative source for key categories and locations. Prioritise adding the highest-search, highest-intent missing entries first. Implement a user-facing 'Report missing place' or 'Suggest an addition' mechanism so gaps are crowd-sourced and prioritised by demand. Set a target coverage rate by category and track it as a product KPI.
acceptance_criteria: Data completeness audit completed comparing platform database against authoritative source for top 1,000 searches
Top 100 missing high-demand entries added within one sprint cycle
'Report missing content' mechanism available to users encountering a not-found result
Coverage rate tracked as a product KPI with a defined target per category
Zero-results rate for known high-intent queries monitored monthly and below 5%
negative_signals: Searching for known high-demand destinations returns correct results
Coverage rate meets defined target for primary categories
User-reporting mechanism available on not-found states
Zero-results rate for known queries below 5%
issues.context_notes: Test by searching for 5–10 known local businesses, venues, or products. Do not flag: Niche or obscure entries that are genuinely unlikely to appear in any platform's database. Industry context: Database incompleteness is a primary driver of churn in navigation apps, local search, and marketplace platforms. Every failed search is a potential competitor switch.

issues.issue_title: Audio instruction contradicts simultaneous visual instruction
issues.user_problem: When an app provides both voice and visual guidance simultaneously, mismatches between the two (e.g., audio says one thing, screen shows another) cause confusion and errors
signals_to_detect: Voice prompt and on-screen directional indicator show conflicting actions at the same moment
Audio confirmation of an action (e.g., 'added to cart') contradicts the visual state shown on screen
Screen reader or assistive audio announces a different state from what is visually displayed
Notification sound plays for an event that is not reflected in the visual UI
Audio description of a UI element's state does not match its visible state
issues.recommendation: Ensure all audio and visual outputs derive from a single shared state object so they can never fall out of sync. Implement automated regression tests that simultaneously capture audio output and screen state for key user flows and flag any mismatch. For screen reader accessibility, ensure all aria-live regions and aria-label values are programmatically linked to the same state variables as the visual components.
acceptance_criteria: Audio and visual instructions derive from a single shared state — no independent audio rendering logic
Automated tests capture and compare audio output against visual state for all primary flows
Zero mismatches between aria-label/aria-live announcements and visible UI state
Manual QA includes a dual-channel check (listen + watch simultaneously) for all guidance-heavy features
User testing with audio-reliant users (eyes-free or screen reader) confirms no instruction conflicts
negative_signals: Audio and visual instructions consistent at all tested interaction points
Shared state object confirmed as single source of truth for both channels
Screen reader and visual display in sync for all interactive states
issues.context_notes: Test by using the app with audio/voice output enabled while observing the screen simultaneously. Do not flag: Minor timing offsets where audio leads or lags visual by under 500ms but conveys the same instruction. Industry context: Audio-visual mismatches are highest-severity in safety-critical contexts (navigation, medical) but also damage trust in any app using voice confirmations, screen readers, or audio feedback.

issues.issue_title: Guidance or direction indicators rendered too late to be actionable
issues.user_problem: Instructions or visual cues that guide a user's next action appear after the decision point has passed, leaving users unable to act on them and causing errors or missed steps
signals_to_detect: Step indicator or progress cue appears only after the user has already passed the relevant point
Warning or alert appears too late for the user to act on it (e.g., stock alert after checkout begins)
Navigation prompt or instruction arrives after the user has already committed to the wrong path
Real-time guidance element has a rendering delay that consistently causes it to display after the action window
Countdown timer or deadline notification appears after the deadline has already passed
issues.recommendation: Audit all time-sensitive guidance elements and define the minimum lead time each requires to be actionable. Optimise rendering pipeline and data fetching to ensure guidance appears within the defined lead time. For critical decision-point instructions, pre-fetch and pre-render content so it is ready before the user reaches the decision point, not fetched on arrival.
acceptance_criteria: All guidance elements appear with sufficient lead time for the user to act on them
Decision-point instructions pre-rendered before the user reaches the relevant screen or moment
Rendering latency for all guidance elements under 300ms from trigger event
QA process includes timing verification — guidance lead time measured and documented for each flow
No user testing session reveals a case where a guidance element appeared after the relevant decision point
negative_signals: All guidance elements appear before the decision point with sufficient lead time
Pre-rendering confirmed for critical path instructions
Rendering latency under 300ms for all guidance elements
issues.context_notes: Test by moving quickly through a flow and noting whether any guidance appears only after you have already passed the relevant point. Do not flag: Confirmations that appear after an action — these are expected post-action feedback, not pre-decision guidance. Industry context: Timing of instructions is critical in navigation apps, checkout flows, booking systems, and any real-time or time-pressured interface.

issues.issue_title: Recalculation or system update delay leaves user in an uncertain state
issues.user_problem: After a user action that requires a system recalculation (route change, price update, availability refresh), the delay is long and silent, leaving the user unsure whether the system is working or has failed
signals_to_detect: After a user action, the interface shows stale data for more than 3 seconds without any loading indicator
Recalculation or refresh takes more than 5 seconds with no progress feedback shown
Users repeat the same action (re-tap, re-search, re-submit) because they cannot tell if the first attempt registered
No 'Updating...' or loading state shown between the user's action and the updated result
ETA, price, or availability estimate not updated after conditions change, showing a stale value without a staleness indicator
issues.recommendation: Show an immediate loading or 'Updating...' state within 200ms of any user action that triggers a recalculation. Set a maximum acceptable recalculation time (e.g., 5 seconds) and display a specific message if the threshold is exceeded (e.g., 'Taking longer than expected — still working'). Where recalculation cannot be instant, show the stale value clearly marked as outdated (e.g., greyed with a refresh icon) until the new value is ready.
acceptance_criteria: Loading or 'Updating...' state displayed within 200ms of any action triggering a recalculation
Stale values clearly marked as outdated while recalculation is in progress
A specific 'Taking longer than expected' message shown if recalculation exceeds 5 seconds
Recalculation completes within 5 seconds under standard network conditions
No user action produces a silent waiting state with no feedback for more than 1 second
negative_signals: Loading state appears immediately on any recalculation-triggering action
Stale values marked as outdated during refresh
Recalculation completes within 5 seconds under standard conditions
No silent waiting states longer than 1 second
issues.context_notes: Test by triggering a recalculation (change a filter, miss a step, modify a basket) and timing how long before updated data appears. Do not flag: Sub-second updates where no loading state is needed. Industry context: Recalculation delays are particularly damaging in booking, pricing, routing, and availability-sensitive contexts where the user's decision depends on the updated value.

issues.issue_title: Stale or outdated data presented as current
issues.user_problem: Users make decisions based on data shown as current (prices, availability, status, time) that is in fact outdated, leading to errors, failed actions, and loss of trust
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Price, stock, or availability shown to user does not match the actual current value at checkout or confirmation
Status indicator (open/closed, available/unavailable) reflects a historical state, not the current state
Data on screen has not refreshed since the page loaded even though underlying conditions have changed
No 'last updated' timestamp or data freshness indicator shown for time-sensitive information
User-submitted action fails because the system has since changed state but the UI did not update
issues.recommendation: Implement automatic data refresh for all time-sensitive values (price, availability, status, ETA) using polling, WebSocket, or server-sent events at an appropriate interval for the context. Display a 'last updated' timestamp on all data where staleness is possible. Where live data is unavailable, clearly mark values as cached or estimated. Set a maximum data age threshold beyond which the value is greyed out and a refresh prompt is shown.
acceptance_criteria: All time-sensitive values (price, availability, status) refresh automatically without manual page reload
Refresh interval appropriate to context: availability every 60s, price every 5 minutes minimum
'Last updated' timestamp shown on all data where staleness is a risk
Cached or estimated values clearly labelled as such — not presented as live
Data older than the defined maximum age shown with a staleness indicator and a refresh prompt
negative_signals: Time-sensitive values refresh automatically at appropriate intervals
Last updated timestamp visible on time-sensitive data
Cached values labelled as such
No reported or observed cases of stale data leading to user errors
issues.context_notes: Test by loading a page and waiting 5+ minutes without refreshing, then checking if values that may have changed (prices, availability, status) are still accurate. Do not flag: Static content (product descriptions, policy text) where staleness in a session is not a UX issue. Industry context: Stale data is a critical issue in availability-sensitive contexts — ticketing, booking, navigation, stock trading, and flash sales.

issues.issue_title: Voice or audio instructions omit key contextual detail
issues.user_problem: Audio instructions are too generic or incomplete, missing specific contextual details (street names, quantities, identifiers) that the user needs to act correctly
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Voice instruction says 'turn right' without naming the street or junction
Audio confirmation says 'item added' without stating which item was added
Screen reader announces a button label ('Submit') without describing what will be submitted
Voice notification says 'your order is ready' without specifying the order number or location
Audio guidance omits numbers, names, or identifiers that would distinguish the correct action from alternatives
issues.recommendation: Audit all voice, audio, and screen reader outputs for completeness. Each instruction should include all identifiers the user needs to act correctly without referencing the screen. Format: action + specific identifier + context (e.g., 'Turn right onto Al Asayel Street in 300 metres', 'Added Blue Wool Coat, size M, to your cart', 'Submit your order of 3 items totalling £47.50'). Update aria-label and aria-live content to include the same specificity.
acceptance_criteria: All voice/audio instructions include specific identifiers (name, number, location) needed to act without visual reference
