Screen reader announcements for actions include the item, quantity, or identifier affected
Audio confirmations for transactions include order number or reference
Aria-label and aria-live content audited to include complete contextual information
Audio instructions tested with eyes-free users — all tested correctly without needing to look at the screen
negative_signals: Voice instructions include specific identifiers at all tested interaction points
Screen reader announcements include item and context detail
Eyes-free testing confirms all audio instructions actionable without visual reference
issues.context_notes: Test with screen reader enabled or voice output active and attempt to complete key flows without looking at the screen. Do not flag: Purely decorative or ambient audio with no instructional purpose. Industry context: Completeness of audio instructions is a WCAG 2.1 requirement for screen reader users and a safety issue for eyes-free mobile contexts (driving, walking).

issues.issue_title: Duplicate UI indicators shown simultaneously with no differentiation
issues.user_problem: The same UI element (icon, badge, label, indicator) appears twice in the same view with identical appearance, causing users to wonder if the duplication is intentional or an error
signals_to_detect: Two identical icons shown side by side or in the same view with no visible difference in state or purpose
The same status badge or label appears in two locations on the same screen showing identical content
Two directional or guidance arrows shown simultaneously with the same label and direction
The same notification or alert shown both inline and in a header badge simultaneously with duplicate content
A UI component rendered twice due to a template or component instantiation error
issues.recommendation: Conduct a page-level audit for any component rendered more than once in the same view. For each duplicate: determine whether both instances are genuinely needed (different context, different state) and if so, differentiate them visually and semantically; or remove one if they serve the same purpose. Primary/secondary patterns should be used when two similar elements are intentionally shown together (e.g., current direction + next direction), with clear visual hierarchy distinguishing them.
acceptance_criteria: No UI element appears twice in the same view with identical appearance and no contextual differentiation
Where two similar elements are intentionally shown, primary/secondary visual hierarchy distinguishes them
Component rendering audited to confirm no template duplication bugs
Each element pair reviewed — documented rationale for any justified repetition
User testing confirms no confusion about duplicate elements in any tested flow
negative_signals: No identical UI elements duplicated in the same view
Intentional similar-element pairs use clear primary/secondary visual hierarchy
No component rendering duplicates identified in template audit
issues.context_notes: Scan each key screen for any component appearing twice. Do not flag: Intentional symmetrical UI design patterns or component repetition across separate sections where context clearly differentiates them. Industry context: Duplicate indicators are most common in dashboard and map interfaces where multiple data layers are rendered independently.

issues.issue_title: Map or spatial UI elements missing contextual labels
issues.user_problem: Visual elements on a map or spatial interface (zones, routes, markers, areas) are not labelled with the information the user needs to identify them, forcing guesswork
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Map route or path shown without street names on the route line
Zones, areas, or regions on a map have no label identifying them
Markers or pins show no tooltip or label on tap/hover
Data visualisation chart shows data points with no axis labels or value labels
Diagram or schematic uses colour-coded areas without a legend or inline labels
issues.recommendation: Label all meaningful elements in spatial and data visualisation UIs directly on or adjacent to the element. For maps: display street names on route lines and zone names on zone overlays. For charts: label axes and key data points. For diagrams: label each zone or region inline. Where space is limited, show labels on tap/hover with a tooltip. Always provide a legend for any colour-coded spatial system.
acceptance_criteria: All routes and paths on maps display street or road names at appropriate zoom levels
All zones, regions, or areas have visible labels either inline or on tap
Chart axes labelled with unit and scale; key data points labelled with values
Diagrams and schematics have inline labels or a legend for all colour-coded elements
Tap/hover tooltips present on all unmarked interactive spatial elements
negative_signals: Street names visible on map route lines
Zone and area labels present on map overlays
Chart axes and key data points labelled
Tap tooltips present on interactive map elements
issues.context_notes: Pan and zoom around the map or spatial UI and check whether meaningful elements have labels. Do not flag: Background decorative map tiles without labels — only navigation-relevant or decision-relevant elements. Industry context: Missing labels are a primary usability issue in navigation, geospatial, logistics, and data visualisation interfaces.

issues.issue_title: Icon colour coding contradicts established conventions in context
issues.user_problem: Icons use colours that contradict the established meaning of those colours in the relevant domain (e.g., traffic, finance, health), causing users to misinterpret status or urgency
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: A green icon used for a warning or error state in a domain where green universally means safe/positive
A red icon used for a positive action or completion state
Traffic or map icons use colours inconsistent with global traffic light conventions (green=clear, amber=slow, red=congested)
Finance or health icons use colours that conflict with domain conventions (red for loss, green for gain in finance)
Icon colour choice tested with users who consistently misread the intended meaning
issues.recommendation: Audit all icon colour usage against domain conventions for the relevant industry. Align icon colours with the established meaning in the user's mental model for that domain. Where a brand colour conflicts with a conventional colour meaning, use the brand colour only for neutral/branding contexts and reserve conventional colours (red, green, amber) for status and severity indicators.
acceptance_criteria: All status and severity icons use domain-conventional colour coding
Brand colours not used for status indicators where they conflict with established conventions
Icon colour audit completed with reference to domain conventions documented
User test with 5 target users confirms all icon colours are interpreted correctly
Icon colour system documented in design system with rationale for each colour assignment
negative_signals: All icon colours aligned with domain conventions
User testing confirms correct interpretation of all icon colours
Brand colours not used for status/severity indicators
issues.context_notes: Compare icon colours against domain conventions (traffic: standard; finance: red=negative, green=positive; health: red=alert). Do not flag: Intentional design decisions where the colour choice is tested and understood by target users. Industry context: Colour convention violations are most severe in safety-critical (navigation, health) and financial contexts where misinterpretation has direct consequences.

issues.issue_title: UI layout or orientation not optimised for secondary display context
issues.user_problem: A UI designed for one display context (handheld phone) is used unchanged in a secondary context (car infotainment, tablet, TV, large screen), resulting in confusing layout, wrong orientation, or unusable interactions
signals_to_detect: App or web UI intended for phone portrait mode appears broken or misaligned in landscape orientation
UI rendered on a car infotainment or tablet screen shows phone-sized elements that are too small to interact with
Progress or directional elements designed for vertical scroll render incorrectly in horizontal display contexts
Touch targets sized for fingertip interaction are too small for cursor or joystick-based infotainment navigation
Content or layout assumes a specific screen size that is not the secondary display context
issues.recommendation: Define all intended display contexts for the product (phone, tablet, car infotainment, desktop, TV) and design or adapt the layout for each. Use responsive design breakpoints for web, and screen size classes for native apps. Test the UI on each target display context specifically — not only on a phone in browser emulation. For car or fixed-display contexts, increase touch/tap target sizes to minimum 80px and prioritise at-a-glance readability.
acceptance_criteria: All intended display contexts identified and listed in the product's design requirements
UI layout tested and functional on each target display context (phone, tablet, infotainment, desktop)
Landscape orientation supported correctly on all mobile screens if the app is used in landscape
Touch targets minimum 80px for car infotainment or cursor-based navigation contexts
No layout breakage, overflow, or misalignment on any supported display context
negative_signals: UI correct and functional on all defined display contexts
Landscape orientation handled correctly
Target sizes appropriate for each interaction mode
No overflow or misalignment on secondary displays
issues.context_notes: Test on the secondary display contexts the product is known or intended to be used on. Do not flag: Products explicitly designed for a single display context only. Industry context: Car infotainment, smart TV, and tablet usage patterns are growing; products that ignore these contexts lose engagement in those channels.

issues.issue_title: 3D or layered UI elements occlude primary content the user needs
issues.user_problem: Three-dimensional rendering, overlapping panels, or layered UI elements cover the primary content (routes, data, text, CTAs) the user needs to see to complete their task
signals_to_detect: 3D building or terrain rendering on a map covers the active route path beneath it
A modal, panel, or overlay partially covers important content without an obvious way to dismiss it
Sticky header or footer obscures interactive elements or body content at certain scroll positions
Floating buttons, tooltips, or badges overlap adjacent CTAs or critical information
Layered UI components (bottom sheets, toasts, drawers) stack on top of each other, hiding content below
issues.recommendation: Apply transparency, ghost rendering, or automatic camera angle adjustment to any 3D elements that occlude user-needed content. For 2D overlays: define a strict z-index management system so layers do not unintentionally stack. Use dynamic positioning for tooltips and floating elements to avoid covering adjacent interactive elements. Audit all sticky and fixed elements at all scroll depths to verify they do not cover body content or CTAs.
acceptance_criteria: Active route, data, or primary content always visible — not covered by 3D elements or overlays
3D elements (buildings, terrain) apply transparency when they would occlude the active path or content
Z-index management system documented and enforced — no unintentional layer stacking
Floating elements (tooltips, buttons, toasts) dynamically positioned to avoid covering adjacent CTAs
Sticky header/footer audit confirms no content or CTAs obscured at any scroll position
negative_signals: Primary content always visible and not occluded by any overlay
3D elements apply transparency when overlapping active content
Z-index system prevents unintentional layer conflicts
Floating elements positioned away from adjacent interactive content
issues.context_notes: Navigate through all key screens and check for any content or CTA being covered by an overlay, sticky element, or 3D rendering. Do not flag: Intentional modal overlays that are clearly designed to focus attention on the overlay content. Industry context: Occlusion issues are most common in map apps, dashboards with data overlays, and interfaces with floating components.

issues.issue_title: Product or service terminology inconsistent between digital and offline channels
issues.user_problem: Users who have encountered a product or service offline (in branch, by phone, in print) use the terminology they heard there, but the digital interface uses different terms for the same things, causing confusion and failed searches
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: A product or feature named differently in the digital interface than it is on physical collateral, by phone agents, or in branch
Users who search for the offline term cannot find the product using that term in the digital channel
Agents and the digital channel use different names for the same account type, product tier, or service
Legal or product documentation uses different terminology from the UI labels for the same items
Translated product names differ between digital and print materials in multilingual markets
issues.recommendation: Conduct a cross-channel terminology audit comparing digital UI labels, phone/branch scripts, print materials, and legal documentation for all product and service names. Produce a single canonical terminology list and enforce it across all channels. For Islamic banking or specialised products, ensure the digital interface uses the same product name as agents and marketing — with a secondary plain-language explanation where needed.
acceptance_criteria: Cross-channel terminology audit completed comparing digital, print, phone, and branch naming
Single canonical product/service name list created and distributed to all channel teams
Searching by offline-used terms in the digital channel returns the correct product or service
Digital UI, agent scripts, and marketing materials use identical product names
Terminology consistency check included in QA for all new product launches and channel updates
negative_signals: Searching by offline product name returns correct digital result
Canonical terminology list exists and is followed across channels
No reported user confusion from terminology differences between channels
issues.context_notes: Test by searching for product names as used in offline collateral and checking if the digital channel recognises them. Do not flag: Minor stylistic differences (capitalisation, abbreviation) that do not affect findability or understanding. Industry context: Particularly impactful in banking, insurance, telecoms, and any regulated industry where product names appear in legal documents.

issues.issue_title: Awareness and educational content absent for unfamiliar product categories
issues.user_problem: Users encountering a product category they are unfamiliar with have no accessible educational content to help them understand what it is, how it works, or why they should consider it
signals_to_detect: Product or service category page has no introductory explanation for users unfamiliar with the category
No 'How it works', 'Why choose X', or beginner guide accessible from the product listing or homepage
Support or FAQ section only accessible from a separate help centre — not linked from the product page
New or specialist product types offered with no comparison to familiar alternatives
Users can proceed to purchase a product they demonstrably do not understand (evidenced by high return rates, high post-purchase support contact, or user testing)
issues.recommendation: Identify the top product or service categories where user unfamiliarity is highest (evidenced by search volume for educational queries, support contacts, or user research). Add an inline educational entry point on each of these category or product pages: a 'How it works' section, a beginner FAQ accordion, or a comparison to familiar alternatives. Make this content accessible without navigating away from the product page.
acceptance_criteria: Educational content ('How it works', FAQ, or comparison) present on all high-unfamiliarity product pages
Educational content accessible from the product page without navigating to a separate help section
Top 5 pre-purchase questions for each unfamiliar category answered inline on the product page
Comparison to familiar alternatives available for products that differ significantly from mainstream equivalents
Educational content coverage measured by reduction in post-purchase support contacts for covered categories
negative_signals: Educational content available on unfamiliar product category pages
Top pre-purchase questions answered inline
Comparison to familiar alternatives available
Reduction in educational support contacts for covered categories
issues.context_notes: Identify the most niche or specialist product categories on the site and check for educational content. Do not flag: Commodity categories where the product type is universally understood. Industry context: Educational content is essential for financial products (investment, Islamic banking, insurance), specialist health products, complex technology, and B2B SaaS.

issues.issue_title: App or product name creates scope confusion about available features
issues.user_problem: The product or app name implies a narrower scope than the product actually covers, causing users to use separate solutions for tasks the product can handle
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: App name refers to one specific feature or use case (e.g., tolls, payments, search) but the app covers significantly broader functionality
Users in research or testing consistently associate the product only with the feature implied by its name
Users switch to a competitor for a task that is available in the product, citing 'this app doesn't do that'
The app's first-launch screen or homepage does not communicate the full range of available features
Feature discoverability research shows high-value features are significantly underused due to unawareness
issues.recommendation: Address scope confusion at the first-launch experience and the app's home screen: communicate the full range of primary features in the onboarding flow and on the home dashboard. If renaming the product is not feasible, use a clear tagline or descriptor that expands the perceived scope (e.g., 'Parking, Tolls & Permits' as a subtitle). Conduct a feature awareness audit to identify which features are underused due to scope misperception and promote them in contextual moments.
acceptance_criteria: First-launch onboarding communicates all primary feature categories to new users
Home screen or dashboard surfaces all primary service categories without requiring navigation
Product descriptor or tagline communicates the full scope of the product beyond the name alone
Feature awareness measured before and after onboarding improvements — underused features show usage uplift
User testing confirms 80%+ of new users correctly identify the full range of primary features after onboarding
negative_signals: Onboarding communicates full feature scope to new users
Home screen surfaces all primary service categories
User testing confirms correct feature awareness post-onboarding
Feature underuse not attributable to unawareness
issues.context_notes: Test by asking 5 new users to list what they think the product does based on the name and first screen alone. Do not flag: Products where the name accurately reflects the intended narrow scope. Industry context: Scope confusion is a significant retention issue in multi-service apps that grew from a single-purpose origin (parking apps that added tolls, ride-hailing apps that added food delivery).

issues.issue_title: Complex system logic or rules not explained at the point of decision
issues.user_problem: Users encounter a system with complex rules (zone types, pricing tiers, eligibility criteria, penalty structures) but receive no contextual explanation at the moment they need to apply those rules
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: A system with multiple zone types, tiers, or categories shows no explanation of the differences at the selection point
Pricing or penalty rules applied automatically with no explanation of how they were calculated
Users make selection errors (wrong zone, wrong tier, wrong option) that could be prevented with a contextual explanation
Help content for complex rules only accessible from a separate FAQ or help centre — not inline
Error messages reference rules without explaining them (e.g., 'This zone requires a permit' with no link to permit information)
issues.recommendation: Map every point in the user journey where complex rules affect the user's decision. At each of these points, add an inline contextual explanation: a tooltip on the zone icon, an expandable info panel on the selection screen, or a 'How this works' link that opens an in-context modal. The explanation should answer: what are the options, how do they differ, and which one is most likely right for the user's situation.
acceptance_criteria: All complex rule-driven decision points have an inline contextual explanation accessible within 1 tap
Explanations answer: what are the options, how do they differ, and what are the consequences of each
Error messages that reference rules include a link to the rule explanation
User testing confirms users can correctly navigate complex rule decisions without contacting support
Support contact rate for rule-related queries measured before and after implementation — target 30% reduction
negative_signals: Inline contextual explanations present at all complex rule decision points
Error messages for rule violations link to the relevant explanation
User testing shows users navigate complex decisions correctly without support
Support contacts for rule-related queries declining
issues.context_notes: Identify the most rule-complex parts of the product (zone selection, tier eligibility, pricing rules, penalty structures) and check for contextual help at those exact points. Do not flag: Simple systems where the rules are self-evident from the UI. Industry context: Contextual rule explanation is critical in government services, transport, regulated financial products, insurance, and multi-tier pricing systems.

issues.issue_title: Real-time availability or live data absent from platform
issues.user_problem: Users need to see current availability (spaces, slots, stock, capacity) before committing to a journey or decision, but the platform shows static or no availability data, forcing them to rely on guesswork or a physical visit
signals_to_detect: Platform shows venues, parking areas, slots, or inventory without any availability indicator
Availability shown is static (always 'Available') regardless of actual real-world conditions
No 'last updated' timestamp on availability data — users cannot assess freshness
Users arrive at a location or attempt a booking only to find it unavailable — information not reflected in the app
Competitor platforms show live availability data for the same locations or items
issues.recommendation: Integrate a real-time availability data feed for all locations, slots, or inventory items where real-time matters for the user's decision. Display availability as a clear indicator (e.g., Available / Limited / Full; Green / Amber / Red) on the selection screen. Show the data freshness timestamp. Where real-time data is not available, show the best available estimate and label it as estimated. Implement a 'Notify me when available' option for currently full/unavailable items.
acceptance_criteria: Availability status shown for all bookable, reservable, or purchasable items where real-time data exists
Availability indicator uses a clear visual system (Available / Limited / Full or equivalent)
Data freshness timestamp shown alongside availability status
Items marked as unavailable cannot be booked or purchased without a confirmation of current status
'Notify me when available' option present for full or unavailable items
negative_signals: Real-time availability shown for all bookable items
Availability indicator uses clear visual system
Data freshness timestamp visible
'Notify me' option available for unavailable items
issues.context_notes: Check whether availability data updates in real time by comparing at different times of day or after known availability changes. Do not flag: Platforms where availability is inherently unlimited or irrelevant (digital downloads, unlimited streaming). Industry context: Real-time availability is table stakes for parking, ticketing, hotel booking, restaurant reservation, and event platforms. Absence is a primary driver of switching to competitors.

issues.issue_title: Missing integration with third-party platforms users rely on
issues.user_problem: Users are forced to context-switch between the product and other essential platforms they use (authentication, payment, related services) because integration is absent, reducing the product's utility and increasing friction
signals_to_detect: Users must log in with separate credentials when a government or social SSO (UAE Pass, Google, Apple ID) is available and expected
Related services from a partner ecosystem not surfaced in-product, requiring users to open a separate app
Payment platform lacks integration with a wallet or payment method widely used by the target audience
Data that users have in a related platform (booking history, account balance, loyalty points) cannot be accessed within this product
Users in research mention switching apps mid-task because integration is absent
issues.recommendation: Conduct a partner ecosystem mapping exercise to identify the top 5 platforms your users rely on alongside your product. Prioritise integrations by: frequency of context-switch (how often users need to go between products), user demand (feature requests, support contacts), and technical feasibility. Build integrations in priority order — starting with SSO (highest impact, reduces sign-up friction), then payment methods, then data sharing. Announce integrations at the point of relevance in the product.
acceptance_criteria: Partner ecosystem map completed identifying top 5 platforms users context-switch to
SSO integration with the most-used authentication platform in the target market (e.g., UAE Pass, Google)
Payment method integration covers the top 3 payment methods used by the target audience
At least one data-sharing integration with a partner platform reduces manual re-entry of existing data
Integration roadmap prioritised and published internally with timeline commitments
negative_signals: SSO with major identity provider available and working
Top payment methods for target market integrated
Partner ecosystem integrations reduce context-switching for key workflows
Integration roadmap in place with prioritised items
issues.context_notes: Interview users or review support contacts to identify which platforms they commonly use alongside this product. Do not flag: Niche integrations requested by a small minority of users — prioritise by demand volume. Industry context: Integration gaps are a significant competitive disadvantage in markets where a dominant platform (UAE Pass, Alipay, Google Pay) has established deep ecosystem expectations.

issues.issue_title: Wide product or service variety undermines perceived specialisation and credibility
issues.user_problem: Users seeing an extremely broad range of offerings assume the platform cannot be expert in all of them, reducing trust in quality
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Platform spans unrelated categories with no clear positioning or specialisation
Homepage shows 20+ unrelated categories with no editorial grouping
No 'About us' or positioning statement explaining the breadth
User research reveals trust concerns related to catalogue breadth
Category pages lack specialist language, curated content, or expertise signals
issues.recommendation: Reframe broad catalogues with a positioning statement that explains the breadth as a deliberate strength. Introduce editorial curation, expert-selected collections, or quality signals (certifications, verified sellers, editorial picks) within each category. Avoid presenting unrelated categories at equal visual weight on the homepage — group or tier them by audience relevance.
acceptance_criteria: Clear value proposition on homepage explains platform breadth as intentional
At least one quality/expertise signal per major category (certifications, expert picks, verified badge)
Homepage categories grouped by user need — not a flat undifferentiated list
User testing confirms breadth does not create trust concerns after positioning improvements
'About us' page accessible from homepage and linked from category pages
negative_signals: Clear positioning statement explains catalogue breadth
Quality signals within categories
Homepage groups categories meaningfully
issues.context_notes: Assess when user research reveals trust concerns related to breadth. Do not flag: established marketplaces where breadth is a known brand value. Industry context: Particularly relevant for newer platforms entering broad categories.

issues.issue_title: Partner or sponsor logos displayed without explaining the relationship
issues.user_problem: Users see recognisable logos and interpret them as endorsements but cannot understand what the partnership means or whether it is relevant to them
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Partner logos displayed with no adjacent label or description
Logo strip labelled only 'Our Partners' with no explanation of contribution
Clicking a logo goes to external website with no in-context explanation
Users in testing cannot explain what the partner relationship means
issues.recommendation: Add a brief descriptor beneath each partner logo explaining the relationship in user-benefit terms (e.g., 'Certified by Google', 'Academic partner'). Group logos under a clear section heading explaining the relationship type. Link each logo to an in-platform explanation page rather than directly to an external site.
acceptance_criteria: Every partner logo has an adjacent label explaining the relationship in plain language
Section heading communicates what the logos represent collectively
Logos link to in-platform explanation pages, not directly external sites
Users in testing correctly describe at least 3 displayed logos
No logo appears without context a first-time user could interpret independently
negative_signals: All logos have descriptors or section heading explains relationship
Links go to in-platform pages
User testing confirms correct interpretation
issues.context_notes: Check homepage and about pages for logo strips. Do not flag: Well-known payment or security badge logos where meaning is universally understood.

issues.issue_title: Low social proof metrics displayed — small numbers create negative impression
issues.user_problem: Displaying enrolment counts, review counts, or purchase numbers when very low has the opposite of the intended effect, reducing trust rather than building it
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Enrolment or purchase count shown below a meaningful threshold (under 50 for courses, under 10 for products)
Review count displayed as '1 review' or '2 reviews' adjacent to the primary CTA
'Be the first to review' shown highlighting absence of social proof
Low buyer counts visible on product cards in listing pages
issues.recommendation: Set minimum display thresholds for social proof metrics: only show enrolment counts above 50, review counts above 10, purchase numbers above 100. Below thresholds, hide the metric entirely or replace with a qualitative signal (e.g., 'New' badge, instructor credentials, platform guarantee). Never display a social proof metric that would actively reduce purchase confidence.
acceptance_criteria: Social proof metrics only shown above defined minimum thresholds
Below threshold: metric hidden or replaced with a non-numerical quality signal
Product cards in listings do not show low counts that would create negative impression
Threshold values documented and enforced across all product types
User testing confirms removal of low-count metrics improves conversion confidence
negative_signals: Social proof metrics only shown above meaningful thresholds
Low counts hidden or replaced with alternative trust signals
No product card shows a count that actively reduces trust
issues.context_notes: Check product cards and PDPs for social proof metrics with value below 10. Industry context: Particularly impactful for new products or marketplace listings where organic traction is still building.

issues.issue_title: Search returns a single detail page instead of a results list
issues.user_problem: When a search has only one matching result, the platform jumps directly to the detail page, bypassing the results list and disorienting users who expected to see results
signals_to_detect: Searching for a term with a single match navigates directly to the detail page with no results list
User taken directly to PDP with no indication a search was performed
No breadcrumb or back-to-results link when arriving at PDP via single-result search
Users must use browser back button to return to search
issues.recommendation: Always return a results page even when there is only one match. Show the single result in the standard results list format with a message such as '1 result for "[term]"'. Reserve direct navigation to a detail page only for exact-ID or barcode lookups where intent is unambiguous.
acceptance_criteria: Searches with a single result show a results page with 1 item — not a direct redirect
Results page shows count ('1 result for X') even for single-match searches
Back navigation from detail page returns user to results page, not homepage
Direct-to-detail navigation only for barcode/exact-ID lookups with clear user intent
User testing confirms no disorientation when a search returns a single result
negative_signals: Single-result searches show a results page not direct redirect
Result count shown even for single results
Back navigation returns to results page
issues.context_notes: Test by searching for a term matching exactly one item. Do not flag: QR/barcode scanning where direct navigation is intentional.

issues.issue_title: Filter option displayed when only 0 or 1 result exists behind it
issues.user_problem: Users select a filter option expecting multiple results but receive 0 or 1, creating disappointment and a sense the filter misled them
signals_to_detect: Filter options displayed with no result count where clicking yields 0 results
A filter category shows options returning only 1 result with no indication of low count
'Free' or 'Special offer' filter exists but applies to only 1 item
Applying filter combinations yields zero results with no feedback before application
issues.recommendation: Show result counts in parentheses next to every filter option, updated dynamically as filters are applied. Disable or mute filter options with 0 results. For options with only 1 result, show the count prominently. Consider hiding filter categories entirely when all their options yield 0 results.
acceptance_criteria: Every filter option shows result count in parentheses (e.g., 'Free (1)')
Filter options with 0 results are visually disabled and non-interactive
Filter options with 1 result show the count clearly before selection
Filter categories where all options yield 0 results are hidden or collapsed
Result counts update dynamically as other filters are applied
negative_signals: Result counts shown next to all filter options
Zero-result options disabled
Single-result options clearly labelled with count
issues.context_notes: Test by checking filter options on a PLP and clicking options that appear to represent a meaningful category but yield only 1 result.

issues.issue_title: Price unit ambiguity on product card — per item, per session, or total unclear
issues.user_problem: Users cannot tell whether the price shown on a card is per lesson, per month, per session, or for the entire product, leading to surprise at checkout
signals_to_detect: Price displayed on product card with no unit qualifier (just '£49' with no 'per month', 'per course', 'total')
Subscription or session-based products show price that could be either recurring or one-time
Price unit differs between product card and detail page
Users in testing express uncertainty about whether price covers the full product or per unit
issues.recommendation: Always accompany prices with a clear unit qualifier on both product cards and PDPs. For single-purchase: 'Total: £49'. For subscriptions: '£49/month'. For session-based: '£10 per session' or '£49 for the full course'. Ensure unit shown on product card exactly matches unit shown at checkout.
acceptance_criteria: Every price on product cards includes a unit qualifier (total, per month, per session, per lesson)
Price unit consistent between product card, PDP, cart, and checkout
Subscription prices clearly show billing frequency
One-time purchase prices clearly labelled as 'total' or equivalent
User testing confirms 100% of users correctly understand what the price covers before clicking through
negative_signals: All prices include clear unit qualifiers
Price unit consistent across card, PDP, and checkout
No user confusion about what the price covers
issues.context_notes: Check product cards for any price shown without a unit qualifier. Industry context: Price unit ambiguity is a primary cart abandonment driver for subscription, course, and service platforms.

issues.issue_title: Progress indicator misread — meaning not self-evident from visual alone
issues.user_problem: Progress bars are misread by users as representing a different metric (upload progress, content availability, or a rating) rather than user completion progress
signals_to_detect: Progress bar present without a text label explaining what it measures
Users in testing describe progress bar as something other than intended
Percentage shown without a 'completed' or 'remaining' qualifier
Progress indicator uses same visual style as a rating or quality metric elsewhere on page
issues.recommendation: Always pair a progress indicator with a plain-language label clarifying what it measures and its direction (e.g., 'Your progress: 40% complete', 'Course completion: 2 of 5 modules done'). Use distinct visual styling for progress indicators vs ratings vs availability meters. If space is limited, add a tooltip or aria-label.
acceptance_criteria: Every progress indicator has an adjacent text label explaining what it measures
Label uses plain language including direction (e.g., 'X% complete', 'X of Y modules done')
Progress indicator visually distinct from rating stars and availability bars
Tooltip or aria-label provides full context on focus/hover
User testing confirms 100% of users correctly interpret progress indicator meaning
negative_signals: All progress indicators have adjacent plain-language labels
Visual style distinct from ratings and availability metrics
User testing shows correct interpretation
issues.context_notes: Check all percentage bars, completion meters, and progress indicators on account, course, and dashboard pages. Industry context: Particularly problematic in learning platforms and dashboards where multiple metric types co-exist.

issues.issue_title: Tab labels not self-explanatory — users must guess what each tab contains
issues.user_problem: Tabs use single-word or icon-only labels that do not communicate their contents clearly, causing users to open tabs speculatively rather than navigating purposefully
signals_to_detect: Tab labels are single ambiguous words (e.g., 'Details', 'Info', 'More') that do not indicate specific content
Icon-only tabs with no text label present
Users in testing open multiple tabs to find content rather than navigating directly
Tab label does not match content found within it
issues.recommendation: Write tab labels that describe their content specifically from the user's perspective (e.g., 'Technical specs', 'Delivery & returns', 'Customer reviews' instead of 'Details', 'Info', 'Reviews'). If tabs use icons, always include a text label. Where a tab contains a count of items, show it (e.g., 'Reviews (124)').
acceptance_criteria: All tab labels describe content specifically — no generic single-word labels
Icon tabs include visible text labels
Tabs with countable content show counts in label
5 users navigate to correct tab for a stated task with 80%+ accuracy
Tab content matches its label — no misleading matches
negative_signals: All tabs have specific, descriptive labels
No icon-only tabs without text
Counts shown where applicable
User testing shows direct tab navigation
issues.context_notes: Check PDP tabs, account section tabs, and any tabbed navigation. Industry context: Ambiguous tabs are a common cause of content not being found, particularly for specifications, policies, and FAQs.

issues.issue_title: Bookmarked or saved items not findable — location does not match user expectation
issues.user_problem: Users who bookmark or save content cannot find it again because it is stored in an unexpected location rather than where they naturally look
signals_to_detect: Bookmarks accessible only from a buried sub-menu rather than account dashboard or main navigation
Saved items section not labelled consistently with the save action label
No persistent link to saved items in global header or account navigation
Users who save an item cannot find it without searching or asking
issues.recommendation: Make saved/bookmarked items accessible from: (1) the primary account navigation menu, and (2) the global header as a bookmark icon on mobile. Ensure the section label exactly matches the action label used throughout the product. On returning to the platform, surface saved items prominently on the user's homepage or dashboard.
acceptance_criteria: Saved/bookmarked items accessible from account navigation within 1 tap
Section label exactly matches the action label used to save the item
Saved items accessible from global header via bookmark/heart icon
Returning users see saved items surfaced on homepage or dashboard
User testing confirms 100% of users locate saved items within 30 seconds
negative_signals: Saved items accessible from account navigation in 1 tap
Section label matches action label
Saved items surfaced for returning users
issues.context_notes: Test by saving an item then navigating away and attempting to find it. Industry context: Save feature utility depends entirely on retrievability — a hard-to-find save feature is unused.

issues.issue_title: Cannot filter or search by content creator, instructor, or author
issues.user_problem: Users who want content from a specific instructor or author cannot filter or search by that person, forcing them to browse all results to find their preferred source
signals_to_detect: No instructor, author, or creator filter available on content listing pages
Search for an instructor name does not surface their content in results
Instructor name links on PDPs do not navigate to a page showing all their content
No 'Browse by instructor' or 'See all from [name]' pathway exists
issues.recommendation: Add an instructor/author/creator filter to all content listing pages. Make instructor names on PDPs clickable links to a profile page showing all their content. Include instructor name in the search index. Consider an 'Instructors' browse section as a primary navigation pathway on platforms where instructor reputation drives purchase decisions.
acceptance_criteria: Instructor/author filter available on all relevant listing pages
Instructor name on PDP is a clickable link to their profile/all-content page
Searching an instructor name returns their content in results
Instructor profile page shows all available content by that creator
'Browse by instructor' pathway accessible from main navigation
negative_signals: Instructor filter available on listing pages
Instructor names are clickable links to profile pages
Instructor search returns correct content results
issues.context_notes: Check whether instructor names are clickable and whether an instructor filter exists. Industry context: On learning platforms, instructor reputation is often the primary purchase driver.

issues.issue_title: No automatic post-completion feedback prompt
issues.user_problem: Users who complete a course, order, or task are not automatically prompted to leave feedback, resulting in low review rates and missed insight
signals_to_detect: No rating or review prompt appears after user completes a purchase, course, or service
Feedback form buried at bottom of page and rarely found organically
No email or push notification prompts review/rating after completion
Users must actively seek the rating mechanism rather than being guided to it
issues.recommendation: Trigger an automatic rating/feedback prompt immediately after the completion event (course completion, order delivery, appointment end). Use a lightweight format: a modal or bottom sheet with a 1–5 star tap plus optional comment field. The prompt should appear in-context and be dismissible. Follow up with an email reminder for users who dismiss without rating within 24–48 hours.
acceptance_criteria: Rating prompt appears automatically within the session after a completion event
Prompt uses lightweight format (star tap + optional comment — no complex form)
Prompt is dismissible with a single tap — never blocks the user
Email reminder sent within 48 hours for users who dismissed the in-app prompt
Review submission rate increases measurably after implementation (target: 3x baseline)
negative_signals: Rating prompt appears automatically post-completion
Prompt is lightweight and dismissible
Email follow-up sent for dismissed prompts
issues.context_notes: Test by completing a course, placing an order, or finishing a service session. Industry context: Completion-triggered prompts generate 3–5x more reviews than passive review links.

issues.issue_title: Review or ratings section present but link to it insufficiently prominent
issues.user_problem: A reviews section exists on the page but the link to it is so low-contrast or small that most users never notice it, missing a key trust signal
signals_to_detect: Star rating near product title is not a clickable link to the reviews section
'View X reviews' link uses muted colour or small font making it visually ignorable
Reviews section at bottom of page but no anchor link brings users there from the top
User testing reveals most users do not discover reviews section despite it being present
issues.recommendation: Make the star rating and review count near the product title a high-contrast, clearly clickable anchor link that smoothly scrolls to the full reviews section. Style the link to look interactive (underline on hover, brand colour). Add a 'Read all reviews' CTA adjacent to the rating count. Ensure the reviews section has a visible section heading reachable via keyboard navigation.
acceptance_criteria: Star rating + review count near product title is a visible clickable anchor link to reviews section
Link text includes review count (e.g., 'Read 48 reviews')
Link uses brand colour or underline to signal interactivity
Smooth scroll to reviews section on click with section heading visible on arrival
User testing shows 80%+ of users discover and access the reviews section when present
negative_signals: Star rating is a clickable link to reviews section
Link includes review count and uses brand colour
Reviews section reachable from anchor link near product title
issues.context_notes: Check whether clicking the star rating near the product title scrolls to the reviews section. Do not flag: Pages where reviews are already visible above the fold.

issues.issue_title: Form or evaluation configured incorrectly prevents users from completing it
issues.user_problem: A form is misconfigured so that users who have answered all questions still cannot proceed or submit, causing frustration and abandonment
nielsen_heuristic: Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors
signals_to_detect: Submit button remains disabled despite user completing all visible fields
Form requires a 'correct' answer to an opinion or feedback question, blocking submission if user's answer is wrong
Per-question 'Send' buttons add friction — user must submit each question individually
Form progress shows incomplete despite all questions being answered
issues.recommendation: Test every feedback, evaluation, and survey form by completing it as a user and verifying the submit path works. Remove any validation logic requiring 'correct' answers on opinion or satisfaction questions. Consolidate per-question submit buttons into a single form-level submit. Ensure all required fields are clearly marked before the user begins.
acceptance_criteria: Completing all visible questions enables submit without error
No validation logic requires a specific answer on open-ended or opinion questions
Single submit button for full form — no per-question submission required
Form tested end-to-end before publication and after any configuration change
Error messages on form submission are specific to the field requiring correction
negative_signals: Form submits successfully after all questions answered
No correct-answer validation on opinion questions
Single submit for entire form
Form tested and verified before deployment
issues.context_notes: Test feedback forms, evaluation forms, and surveys by completing them fully. Industry context: Incorrectly configured feedback forms are a common LMS and CRM issue.

issues.issue_title: Feature visible in UI but not actionable — no clear next step
issues.user_problem: A feature or section is displayed in the interface but provides no clear call to action, leaving users uncertain what to do with it
signals_to_detect: A section or widget in the UI shows a feature name but has no CTA or interaction
Feature displayed in navigation opens to an empty or unexplained state
Progress planner or dashboard widget visible but has no input mechanism
Clicking a feature opens a page showing a concept but does not guide user on how to use it
issues.recommendation: Every feature presented in the UI must have at minimum one explicit primary action that initiates or advances its use. Apply the principle: show the feature only when the user can take a meaningful action with it right now. For features requiring setup, show a guided first-use prompt. For features with multiple steps, show the specific next step the user needs to take from their current state.
acceptance_criteria: Every displayed feature has a primary CTA or action trigger visible on the same screen
Features in setup state show an explicit 'Get started' or first-step prompt
Features requiring data input show the input mechanism immediately
User testing confirms users can identify and execute the next action for every displayed feature
No section or widget renders as display-only with no interaction pathway
negative_signals: All displayed features have a primary action CTA
Setup-state features show guided first-use prompt
No display-only widgets with no interaction pathway
issues.context_notes: Check account dashboards, onboarding flows, and recently added features. Industry context: Display-only features are common in MVP launches where UI was built before backend was ready.

issues.issue_title: Status icon meaning unclear — users cannot interpret what it represents
issues.user_problem: An icon used to indicate a status has no label or tooltip, leaving users guessing what it means
signals_to_detect: Tick, check, cross, lock, or warning icon used without a text label or tooltip
Status icon interpretation varies across users
Hovering or tapping icon produces no tooltip or explanation
Same icon used in different contexts with different meanings
issues.recommendation: Add a visible text label adjacent to all status icons, or a tooltip that appears on hover/focus. For icon-heavy interfaces, add an 'icon legend' section in onboarding or accessible help panel. Ensure each icon is used consistently for only one meaning across the entire platform.
acceptance_criteria: All status icons have an adjacent text label or tooltip explaining their meaning
Tooltip appears on hover/tap within 300ms for all icon-only indicators
Icon legend provided in onboarding or accessible help panel for icon-heavy interfaces
Each icon used for only one meaning — no context-dependent reuse
User testing confirms 100% of users correctly interpret all status icons after implementation
negative_signals: All status icons have labels or tooltips
Icons used consistently for one meaning only
User testing confirms correct interpretation
issues.context_notes: Check module completion ticks, lock icons, bookmark indicators, and status badges. Do not flag: Universally recognised icons (play button, pause, close X).

issues.issue_title: Horizontal scroll used as primary navigation pattern on mobile
issues.user_problem: Users are expected to scroll horizontally to browse the main content or navigation on mobile, which is not a standard discoverable interaction pattern and causes content to be missed
signals_to_detect: Homepage requires horizontal swiping to access primary navigation categories
Primary content in horizontal scroll container with no visual affordance of scrollability
Category filter row is fully horizontal with no fallback vertical view
Users in testing miss content in horizontal scroll because they do not attempt the swipe gesture
No visible indicator (progress dots, partial card bleed) communicating more content exists horizontally
issues.recommendation: Replace horizontal scroll as a primary navigation pattern with a vertical list or grid. Reserve horizontal scroll for supplementary carousels where: (1) a partial next card is visible as affordance, (2) the content is not the primary pathway, and (3) the full item count is communicated. For category navigation on mobile, use a vertical accordion, a 2-column grid, or a sticky filter row.
acceptance_criteria: Primary category navigation on mobile uses vertical list or grid — not horizontal scroll
Any horizontal scroll shows partial next item as visual affordance
Horizontal scroll limited to supplementary content (carousels, brand logos, tags)
All primary content pathways accessible via vertical scroll without horizontal interaction
User testing confirms no key content missed due to undetected horizontal scroll
negative_signals: Primary navigation uses vertical list or grid on mobile
Horizontal scrolls show partial next item affordance
No primary pathway requires horizontal interaction
issues.context_notes: Check mobile homepage and category pages at 375px. Do not flag: Supplementary horizontal carousels with visible partial cards and dot indicators.

issues.issue_title: Promotion or ad leads to a page with no purchase CTA
issues.user_problem: Users who click a promotional banner arrive on a page that provides information but has no Add to Cart or Buy CTA, creating a dead end for purchase intent
signals_to_detect: Clicking a promotional banner leads to a product feature or brand story page with no purchase CTA
An ad or offer tile leads to a category or editorial page where no items can be added to cart
'Learn more' CTA on promotional product tile links to a static information page
Promotional destination page has no 'Shop now', 'Add to Cart', or 'View product' CTA
issues.recommendation: Every promotional banner, ad tile, and offer CTA must lead to a page where the user can take a purchase action within 1–2 clicks. If destination is a brand or feature page, add a 'Shop [Brand/Category]' CTA or embedded product carousel with Add to Cart. Audit all promotional destinations before publishing any campaign.
acceptance_criteria: Every promotional banner leads to a page with Add to Cart or View product CTA visible above the fold
Brand and feature pages linked from promotions include a purchase pathway
Pre-publish audit checklist for campaigns includes verification of purchase CTA on destination
No promotional destination is a static information page with no purchase action
Analytics confirms reduced drop-off after adding purchase CTAs to promotional destinations
negative_signals: All promotional CTAs lead to pages with purchase pathway
Brand/feature pages include product carousel or 'Shop now' CTA
Campaign audit checklist in place
issues.context_notes: Click every promotional banner on homepage and PLP and check whether destination has a purchase CTA above the fold.

issues.issue_title: Global navigation repeated inside subcategory pages causing confusion
issues.user_problem: The same top-level navigation that appears on the homepage also appears inside deep category pages, causing users to accidentally navigate back to the top level when trying to browse within their current category
signals_to_detect: Top-level global navigation visible on a deep category page alongside category-specific navigation
Clicking a category from global nav while inside a subcategory resets user to top level
Category page has two navigation systems active simultaneously creating visual clutter
Users in testing accidentally navigate back to home category when intending to stay in current subcategory
issues.recommendation: On category and subcategory pages, collapse or replace the global navigation to show only: logo, search, cart, and account icons — removing the full category menu. Use breadcrumbs and contextual sidebar/filter navigation for movement within the current category hierarchy. The full global navigation should only be accessible via a menu icon, not persistently displayed on category pages.
acceptance_criteria: Global category navigation collapsed or hidden on category and subcategory pages
Only logo, search, cart, and account icons persist in header on category pages
Breadcrumbs provide navigation up the category hierarchy
Category-level navigation (subcategories, filters) provided contextually on the page
User testing confirms no accidental navigation back to home level when browsing within a category
negative_signals: Global nav collapsed on subcategory pages
Breadcrumbs provide contextual hierarchy navigation
Category browsing does not accidentally reset to top level
issues.context_notes: Navigate to a third-level category page and check whether the full global nav is still showing. Do not flag: Sites with a single-level navigation where no hierarchy conflict exists.

issues.issue_title: Filter application yields zero results with no guidance on what to do next
issues.user_problem: Users apply a filter combination that returns zero results and receive no explanation of why or what they should do to find products
nielsen_heuristic: Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors
signals_to_detect: Applying a filter combination results in an empty product grid with no message
Zero results page shows only blank area or generic 'No products found' with no recovery options
No suggestion to remove filters, broaden criteria, or explore related categories
Applied filters not shown as removable chips on zero results state
No 'Clear filters' CTA visible when zero results is shown
issues.recommendation: Design a dedicated zero-results filter state that: (1) explains which filters caused empty results, (2) shows applied filters as removable chips, (3) suggests the most-likely fix, (4) shows popular products in the category as alternatives, (5) includes a 'Clear all filters' CTA. Never show a blank page.
acceptance_criteria: Zero-results filter state shows clear message explaining no products match current filters
Applied filters visible as removable chips on zero-results state
'Clear all filters' CTA prominent on zero-results state
At least one alternative pathway offered (related products, broader category, or suggested filter change)
No blank page or generic error — zero results state is a designed UI state
negative_signals: Zero-results state shows explanation and recovery options
Applied filters shown as removable chips
'Clear all filters' CTA present
Alternatives or suggestions provided
issues.context_notes: Test by applying multiple filters that in combination yield no results. Industry context: Filter zero-results without recovery is a top-5 most common PLP usability failure.

issues.issue_title: Full-screen overlay used for a minor action that only warrants a half-screen drawer
issues.user_problem: A modal takes over the entire screen for a simple selection or confirmation action, blocking all context and making the interaction feel disproportionately heavy
signals_to_detect: A full-screen modal appears for an action involving fewer than 5 options or a single confirmation
A bottom drawer expands to 100% of the viewport for a minor selection (quantity, add-on, colour)
Content within the full-screen overlay is minimal leaving large empty areas
Dismissing the overlay requires a swipe or small close icon — no tap-outside-to-close
Users in testing express surprise at scale of overlay for a minor action
issues.recommendation: Use full-screen modals only for complex multi-step flows or content-heavy overlays that genuinely require full focus. For minor selections, use a bottom sheet capped at 50% of screen height. Ensure all overlays: (1) can be dismissed by tapping outside the sheet, (2) have a visible close control, (3) have a handle indicating dismissibility on mobile.
acceptance_criteria: Overlays for minor selections (under 5 options) use half-screen bottom sheet not full screen
Full-screen modals reserved for complex multi-step flows only
All bottom sheets dismissible by tapping outside the sheet area
Bottom sheet height does not exceed 60% of viewport for simple selections
User testing shows no frustration or surprise at overlay scale for common actions
negative_signals: Minor selections use appropriately sized bottom sheets
Full-screen modals only used for genuinely complex flows
All overlays dismissible by tapping outside
issues.context_notes: Check all modals and drawers triggered by Add to Cart, quantity selection, and add-on offers. Do not flag: Full-screen modals for multi-step flows that genuinely require full focus.

issues.issue_title: Quantity sold only in multiples — unit convention not communicated to user
issues.user_problem: Products sold in pairs, packs, or bundles display quantity selectors in multiples without explaining the convention, leaving users confused about whether they are ordering 2 items or 1 pack of 2
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Quantity selector increments in multiples of 2 or more with no label explaining why
Product title or description does not state it is sold in pairs, packs, or bundles
Cart shows quantity as '2' but user intended to order '1 pack of 2'
Minimum order quantity greater than 1 with no explanation
Price shown per unit but product sold in multiples — effective unit price never stated
issues.recommendation: State the unit convention explicitly in the product title or adjacent to the price (e.g., 'Sold as a pair', 'Pack of 6', 'Minimum order: 2'). Display the quantity selector in individual units (1, 2, 3 = 1 pair, 2 pairs, 3 pairs) with a note explaining the pack size. Show the per-unit and per-pack price clearly.
acceptance_criteria: Product title or adjacent label states the selling unit (pair, pack, bundle, minimum quantity)
Quantity selector uses individual units with a pack-size note (e.g., '1 = 1 pair of 2 items')
Cart displays the pack convention so users can verify their order
Per-unit and per-pack pricing both shown where relevant
User testing confirms 100% of users understand the quantity convention before purchase
negative_signals: Selling unit stated in product title or adjacent label
Quantity selector uses individual units with pack-size note
Cart confirms pack convention clearly
issues.context_notes: Check products with multi-unit selling conventions (pairs, packs, bulk). Industry context: Quantity convention confusion leads to over-ordering and returns in categories like hosiery, batteries, and food.

issues.issue_title: Loyalty or rewards feature benefit not explained before sign-up CTA
issues.user_problem: Users are prompted to sign up for a loyalty scheme without first being told what benefits it provides, reducing motivation to engage
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: 'Apply for rewards card' CTA shown with no adjacent benefit statement
Benefits of membership only accessible after clicking 'Learn more' or a separate page
Loyalty scheme mentioned in navigation without explaining what it offers
Users in testing cannot explain what a loyalty card offers without investigating further
Sign-up form asks for personal details before any benefit is communicated
issues.recommendation: Precede every loyalty sign-up CTA with a concise benefit statement listing the top 2–3 tangible benefits (e.g., 'Earn 1 point per £1 spent, redeem for discounts, get exclusive member offers'). Use a benefit summary card or 3-icon feature grid immediately above the CTA. Never ask users to sign up without first communicating the value they receive.
acceptance_criteria: Benefits statement with top 2–3 specific benefits visible immediately above every loyalty sign-up CTA
Benefit summary accessible without clicking away from current page
Benefits stated in concrete terms not vague ('great benefits')
Sign-up form not shown before benefit explanation is seen
User testing confirms users can state at least 2 loyalty benefits before clicking the sign-up CTA
negative_signals: Benefit statement with specific details visible above sign-up CTA
Benefits accessible without navigating away
Users can state benefits before committing to sign-up
issues.context_notes: Check loyalty card sections and any membership sign-up CTAs. Industry context: Unexplained loyalty sign-up CTAs have very low conversion — benefit communication immediately above the CTA is the single highest-impact fix.

issues.issue_title: In-app content opens in external webview without warning
issues.user_problem: Users navigating within an app are unexpectedly taken to an external browser for certain pages, losing their app context and navigation state
signals_to_detect: Tapping a menu item, policy link, or feature opens the device browser instead of an in-app page
Browser header replaces app navigation — losing back button and in-app context
No warning that a link will open outside the app
Closing external browser returns user to home screen or loses navigation state
Back navigation from webview does not return user to where they were in the app
issues.recommendation: Migrate all policy, help, and support content to native in-app pages following the app's design system. For content that must remain on the web, use an in-app browser (SFSafariViewController on iOS, Chrome Custom Tabs on Android) with a persistent 'Back to [App Name]' button. Always warn users before leaving the app context if an external browser is unavoidable.
acceptance_criteria: Terms, policies, and help content displayed as native in-app pages
No in-app navigation results in unexpected external browser launch
If external browser unavoidable, an in-app browser with back navigation is used
Users can return to their previous in-app position after viewing external content
User testing confirms no navigation context lost when accessing policies or help content
negative_signals: All in-app content rendered as native pages
External links open in in-app browser with back navigation
No unexpected browser launches from within the app
issues.context_notes: Tap all policy links, T&C links, and help centre links within the app. Do not flag: Intentional 'share' or 'open in browser' actions initiated by the user.

issues.issue_title: Back button disappears or becomes non-functional on certain pages
issues.user_problem: Users attempting to navigate back from a page cannot do so because the back button has disappeared or stopped working, trapping them in the current view
signals_to_detect: Back button disappears from the navigation bar on certain page types (PDP, webview, modal)
Tapping the back button produces no navigation response
Back navigation works on most pages but fails after certain actions (log in, payment, webview transition)
Hardware back button on Android does not match in-app back button behaviour
Users must use workarounds (swipe gesture, long-press history) to go back from certain pages
issues.recommendation: Audit all page transitions to ensure the back button is present and functional on every page. For pages opened via webview or modal, implement explicit back navigation returning users to their prior in-app state. Test back navigation specifically after: login, payment completion, webview transitions, and deep link arrivals. Implement onBack handlers for Android hardware back button parity.
acceptance_criteria: Back button present and functional on all page types
Back navigation tested and confirmed working after login, payment, and webview transitions
Android hardware back button behaviour mirrors in-app back button on all pages
No page traps the user with no back navigation
Back navigation QA included in release checklist for every new page template
negative_signals: Back button present and functional on all tested pages
Back navigation confirmed after all major transitions
Android hardware back button parity confirmed
issues.context_notes: Test back navigation from every page type, particularly after login, webview, and payment flows. Do not flag: Intentional pages with no back (e.g., order confirmation where back would re-submit payment).

issues.issue_title: Discount displayed as a positive number instead of negative
issues.user_problem: Discounts shown as '30%' instead of '−30%' are less immediately readable as a saving and can be confused with a markup or product attribute
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Discount percentage shown as '30%' without minus sign or 'off' qualifier
Sale badge shows '30%' next to product without communicating it is a reduction
Discount in cart shown as positive number in the price breakdown
Promotional savings displayed inconsistently (some '−30%', some '30% off', some '30%')
issues.recommendation: Standardise all discount displays to use a negative format: '−30%' for percentage discounts, or '−£15.00' for absolute savings. Alternatively, use 'Save 30%' or '30% off'. Apply consistently across product cards, PDPs, cart, and checkout. Never show a discount as a bare positive percentage that could be misread.
acceptance_criteria: All discount percentages shown with minus sign (−30%) or 'off'/'save' qualifier (30% off, Save 30%)
Format consistent across product cards, PDPs, cart, and checkout
No bare positive percentage used for a discount without a qualifier
Discount format tested with 5 users who all immediately identify it as a saving
Consistency audit completed across all page types showing discounts
negative_signals: All discounts shown with minus sign or 'off'/'save' qualifier
Format consistent across all pages
User testing confirms immediate recognition as a saving
issues.context_notes: Check PLP product cards, PDP pricing, and cart line items for discounts shown without minus or qualifier.

issues.issue_title: Address form field label too specific — excludes valid address types
issues.user_problem: An address form field labelled with a specific term (e.g., 'Building number') does not accommodate other valid address types (villas, houses), causing confusion for users whose address doesn't fit the label
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Address field labelled 'Building number' when villas and houses are common in the market
Form asks for 'Apartment number' without a villa/house alternative
Address type field only offers 'Apartment' and 'Office' with no 'Villa', 'House', or 'Other' option
Users in testing express confusion about filling address fields for non-apartment residences
issues.recommendation: Use generic, inclusive labels for address fields: 'Address line 1', 'Address line 2 (optional)' or 'Building/Villa/House number'. Where an address type selector is provided, include all common address types for the target market. For Middle East markets specifically, include Villa and Compound as primary options.
acceptance_criteria: Address field labels are generic and inclusive of all residential types in the target market
Address type selector includes Villa, House, and Compound options for relevant markets
Form tested with villa and compound addresses — all fields completable without workaround
Labels updated to use inclusive terminology
Address form validated by a user from each primary residential type in the target market
negative_signals: Address labels inclusive of all residential types
Address type selector includes Villa and Compound for relevant markets
All address types completable without confusion
issues.context_notes: Check address form field labels in checkout. Particularly important in GCC markets (UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar) where villa and compound living is very common.

issues.issue_title: Single available option presented as a choice — false decision forced on user
issues.user_problem: Users are shown a selection step with only one option available, forcing them to select it as if it were a choice — adding friction without providing any control
signals_to_detect: Shipping method selector shows only one option — user must select it to proceed
Payment method step shows one option requiring user to click it before continuing
Date or time picker presents one available slot — user must select the predetermined option
A dropdown or radio group with one item forces user interaction with no real decision
issues.recommendation: When only one option exists for a selection step, auto-select it and skip the explicit selection interaction. Display it as informational text rather than a selector: 'Shipped via Standard Delivery'. Only render a selection UI when there are 2 or more genuine options. If more options are coming, hide the step entirely rather than showing a placeholder.
acceptance_criteria: Single-option steps auto-selected and shown as confirmation text, not as selection UI
Checkout steps with one option do not require user interaction to proceed
Shipping method, payment method, and date steps show selectors only when 2+ options exist
Informational display of pre-selected single options uses clear language
User testing shows no unnecessary decision fatigue from single-option steps
negative_signals: Single-option steps auto-selected and shown as informational text
No selection UI rendered for fewer than 2 options
Checkout tested with 1-option steps confirmed as auto-selected
issues.context_notes: Check checkout shipping and payment steps for single-option selectors. Industry context: False choices in checkout add unnecessary steps that inflate perceived checkout complexity.

issues.issue_title: App store listing does not articulate app benefits — low motivation to download
issues.user_problem: Users viewing the app in the app store see a generic description and low-quality screenshots that do not communicate why the app is worth downloading
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: App store description is generic — does not list specific features or benefits over mobile website
App store screenshots show default screens rather than feature highlights with annotated benefits
No preview video in the app store listing
App store rating below 4.0 with unaddressed negative reviews about core features
App store description not updated in over 6 months despite new features added
issues.recommendation: Rewrite the app store description to lead with the top 3 user benefits in plain language. Update screenshots to use annotated benefit-highlight format. Add a preview video showing the core user journey. Respond to all recent negative reviews with acknowledgement and resolution status.
acceptance_criteria: App store description leads with 3 specific user benefits in first 2 lines
Screenshots use annotated feature-highlight format with benefit callouts
Preview video present showing core user journey in under 30 seconds
App store rating 4.0 or above with a response to all reviews in last 90 days
App store listing updated within 2 weeks of any major feature release
negative_signals: App store description leads with specific user benefits
Screenshots use feature-highlight format
Preview video present
Rating 4.0+ with recent review responses
issues.context_notes: Review the app's App Store and Google Play listing pages. Industry context: App store listings are often neglected post-launch — they are a key acquisition channel.

issues.issue_title: User-generated content not filtered for PII — personal contact details exposed in reviews
issues.user_problem: Users who post their email address or phone number in a review expose their personal contact information publicly, creating a privacy and safety risk
signals_to_detect: Review or comment text contains email address format (user@domain.com) or phone number patterns
No pre-publication content filter for personal information in user-generated content fields
PII visible in published reviews without redaction
Review submission form has no warning that personal information should not be included
issues.recommendation: Implement automated PII detection on all user-generated content before publication. Use regex patterns to detect email addresses, phone numbers, and national ID formats — redact or flag them for human review before going live. Add a pre-submission notice: 'Do not include personal contact information — it will be visible publicly.' Retroactively scan and redact existing PII in published reviews.
acceptance_criteria: Automated PII detection active on all review, comment, and Q&A submission flows
Email addresses and phone numbers in review text automatically redacted before publication
Pre-submission warning displayed on all UGC input forms
Retroactive PII scan and redaction completed on all published content
Moderation workflow flags any PII not caught by automated filters within 24 hours
negative_signals: PII detection active on all UGC fields
Pre-submission warning displayed
No personal contact details visible in published reviews
issues.context_notes: Check published reviews for email address or phone number patterns. Industry context: PII exposure in UGC is a GDPR/data protection violation.

issues.issue_title: Voting or rating other users' reviews causes confusion
issues.user_problem: The ability to give a star rating to another user's review is confusing — users are unsure whether they are rating the product or the helpfulness of the review
signals_to_detect: Star rating control present on individual review cards — not on the product itself
Review helpfulness voting uses 1–5 star format rather than simple upvote/downvote
Tapping a star on a review card is ambiguous — users unsure if rating review or product
Review helpfulness interaction labelled ambiguously
