The collapsed icon must not cover interactive content — position it in the bottom corner (bottom-right for LTR, bottom-left for RTL) and account for bottom navigation bars. Never use an expanded default state for floating widgets on content or product pages. On checkout and form pages, consider hiding floating elements entirely.
acceptance_criteria: All floating widgets have a visible collapse/minimise button that reduces them to a small icon
Collapsed icon does not cover any CTA, interactive element, or critical content
Collapsed state persists for the session — widget does not re-expand on page change unless user explicitly opens it
On mobile, the floating icon does not overlap with bottom navigation or sticky Add to Cart bars
Floating elements hidden or collapsed by default on checkout and form pages
negative_signals: Floating widgets collapsible to small icon
Collapsed icon covers no interactive content
Collapsed state persists across pages
Hidden on checkout and form pages
issues.context_notes: Check all pages for floating elements and verify they can be minimised. This is distinct from UX-101 (intrusive chat appearing immediately — timing issue) and UX-243 (multiple simultaneous overlays). This is specifically about a persistent, non-dismissible floating element that cannot be collapsed. Do not flag: Floating elements that are dismissible or already collapsed by default. Industry context: Non-collapsible chat widgets from third-party providers (Intercom, Zendesk, Freshchat) are the most common source of this issue — they often have collapse disabled in configuration.

issues.issue_title: Non-interactive UI element styled to look clickable — misleads users into attempting interaction
issues.user_problem: A banner, label, or highlighted element uses visual styling (blue colour, underline, border) that signals interactivity, but clicking or tapping it produces no response, confusing users and eroding trust
signals_to_detect: A banner, label, or section uses brand colour (e.g., blue) for a purely informational element, causing it to appear as a clickable link or button
Users tap or click a highlighted element expecting navigation or an action, but nothing happens
An element uses an underline, border, or interactive visual treatment that is not accompanied by a click handler
Users in testing report clicking on elements that are not interactive and expressing confusion
The element uses the same visual style as nearby interactive elements but is not itself interactive
issues.recommendation: Reserve interactive visual styles (brand colour text, underlines, button borders, hover states) exclusively for elements that trigger an action. For informational elements that should be visually prominent but are not interactive, use a distinct visual treatment: a coloured background block, an icon, or a different typeface weight — without the link/button affordances. Conduct a systematic audit of all coloured or highlighted non-interactive elements across the site.
acceptance_criteria: No non-interactive element uses a visual style associated with clickable links or buttons on the same page
Colour used exclusively for interactive elements is not used for purely informational content
Audit completed of all highlighted/coloured elements — each categorised as interactive or informational with appropriate styling
Design system documents which visual treatments are interactive vs informational
User testing confirms zero instances of users clicking on non-interactive elements expecting a response
negative_signals: All interactive visual styles exclusive to clickable elements
No informational elements using button/link affordances
Audit completed and design system documents interactive vs informational treatments
issues.context_notes: Systematically tap/click all visually prominent elements (coloured, bordered, highlighted) on key pages and note which produce no response. Do not flag: Elements that are interactive but produce a small or subtle response the user might miss — that is a feedback issue, not a false affordance issue. Industry context: False affordances (non-interactive elements that look interactive) are common when brand colour is also the link colour — a design system convention mismatch.

issues.issue_title: Unavailable payment option shown without explanation of why it is unavailable
issues.user_problem: A payment option is visible on the payment selection screen but is greyed out or disabled with no explanation of why it cannot be selected, causing confusion and preventing users from understanding their alternatives
nielsen_heuristic: Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors
signals_to_detect: A payment method option is visually greyed out or disabled on the payment selection screen
No tooltip, label, or inline explanation for why the payment option is unavailable
Users in testing tap the greyed option expecting to use it and receive no feedback
Payment option unavailable due to order value, region, or product type — but no reason communicated
Disabled payment option has the same visual weight as available options, making it ambiguous rather than clearly unavailable
issues.recommendation: For any payment option that is displayed but currently unavailable, explain why: show a brief inline label beneath the greyed option (e.g., 'Not available for orders over SAR 5,000', 'Not available in your region', 'Not available for this product type'). If the reason cannot be disclosed, use 'Currently unavailable'. Alternatively, hide payment options that are completely irrelevant to the user's current order rather than showing them as disabled. Never show a greyed option with no explanation.
acceptance_criteria: Every disabled or greyed payment option shows an inline explanation of why it is unavailable
Explanation text appears below or adjacent to the disabled option — not only on hover
If the reason cannot be stated, 'Currently unavailable' is used as a minimum fallback
Payment options that are permanently unavailable for the current context are hidden, not shown as disabled
User testing confirms users understand why their preferred payment option is unavailable
negative_signals: All disabled payment options show an explanation label
Explanation visible without hover or tap
Users in testing understand why unavailable options cannot be selected
issues.context_notes: Check the payment selection step of checkout for any greyed or disabled payment options. Do not flag: Payment options that are fully hidden when unavailable — only flag when shown in a disabled state without explanation. Industry context: Unexplained disabled payment options are common in platforms that support instalment or BNPL options with minimum order requirements — users who do not meet the threshold see the option as disabled with no explanation.

issues.issue_title: Product card or listing image depicts multiple products but title and price describe only one
issues.user_problem: The product image shows a bundle, set, or multiple items together, but the product title and price only describe or apply to a single item — users believe they are buying all items shown in the image
nielsen_heuristic: Match between system and real world
signals_to_detect: Product listing image shows a phone with accessories (case, charger, earphones) but price and title are for the phone alone
PDP hero image shows a set or bundle but 'What's in the box' only contains the primary item
Multiple products visible in the main image with no label clarifying which item the listing is for
Users in testing express surprise or disappointment when they discover the accessories shown are not included
Image is a lifestyle shot with incidental products that users mistake for included items
issues.recommendation: Ensure the primary product image on PLPs and PDPs accurately represents only what is included in the purchase. Do not use images showing accessories, complementary products, or lifestyle context items unless they are explicitly included. If a lifestyle image must be used, add an overlay label: 'Accessories not included' or 'Sold separately'. On PDPs, ensure the 'What's in the box' section matches exactly what is depicted in the product images.
acceptance_criteria: Primary product image on PLP card and PDP shows only the product being sold — no additional items that are not included
If lifestyle or context images are used, an 'Accessories not included' label is clearly visible
'What's in the box' section on PDP matches exactly what is shown in the product images
Image review checklist includes verification that no non-included items are shown as part of the product
User testing confirms zero misunderstanding about what is included in the purchase price
negative_signals: Product images show only items included in purchase
Lifestyle images labelled 'Accessories not included'
What's in the box matches product images
User testing shows correct understanding of included items
issues.context_notes: Check PLP cards and PDPs — particularly for electronics and tech products where accessories are commonly shown with the main product. Do not flag: Clearly labelled bundle or kit listings where all shown items are included and the title/price reflect the bundle. Industry context: Misleading product images are one of the primary causes of returns in electronics — customers who receive only the device when the image showed device + accessories feel deceived.
